speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today in recognition of International Women's Day, a day which gives us an opportunity to pay tribute to the progress women have made collectively and individually.
Since the early 1970s when the women's movement began in earnest, women have organized and worked effectively for social and economic change. Since the early part of the century, March 8 has increasingly become a focal point for drawing attention to women's concerns.
Across Canada this week, more than 900 groups representing women from farms to cities are going beyond simply celebrating the day; they are organizing activities around issues that are so crucial to their struggle for equality.
[ Translation]
This year, International Women's Day has particular significance.

Indeed, it falls in the year marking the culmination of the United Nations "Decade for Women". In July, Canada will join with other countries in a world conference on women which will be taking place in Nairobi, Kenya.
The concerns and achievements of Canadian women will be brought to the conference table and shared with women from around the world who are part of this global struggle for equality.
The concerns of women are many and varied. In Ethiopia, for example, there is the tragic famine. In many Third World nations women are plagued by poverty and illiteracy. Indeed, the needs of women in the developing world are dramatic, but the needs of women in Canada are great too.

With great respect to the Minister, I am now in some difficulty because this is the period for 90-second statements. May I take it that the Minister was rising to seek unanimous consent of the House that we move to Statements by Ministers? Is there unanimous consent for that?
No.
There is not unanimous consent. I must advise the Minister that his 90 seconds have expired.

subsubtopic: SITUATION OF IMMIGRANT WOMEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on International Women's Day, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the lives of immigrant women in Canada. Many are confined to jobs in the lowest-paying industries in our country, services and manufacturing, which employ one-third of immigrant women, compared with one-fifth of all Canadian women and one-sixth of all Canadian men. Language training courses do not always fit in with their working hours, and there is a serious lack of industrial training courses.
Many of these women work in the home and are not eligible for language training because the programs are offered only to individuals who intend to enter the labour market.
There is a great deal to improve in our adjustment and training courses for immigrant women, and I think an approach based on feminine values and a more generous and humanitarian outlook would be advisable for these programs.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to join my colleagues in paying tribute to women around the world and women in Canada on the 75th anniversary of International Women's Day. Women in Canada have contributed much, in building this country originally as pioneers, as farm women, as homemakers, as workers in many fields of endeavour, and as those who perhaps contributed most to the survival of families during the Great Depression, which was followed by the war. We are now in the forefront of maintaining peace as well as contributing to our social and economic well-being.
Our heritage has been enriched, particularly by the contribution of Inuit and Indian women and the different cultures

March 8, 1985
and viewpoints brought by women from many countries. It has been through hard work of Canadian women that we have achieved victories such as equal pay for equal value, although much remains to be done-legislation outlawing discrimination on the basis of sex, recognition of society's contribution to children through some form of maternity benefits and, if not action, at least acknowledging the lack of truly equal opportunities and the systemic barriers facing women.
We are looking forward to really establishing equality under the Charter of Rights, with sound amendments that will benefit women and implement equality. International Women's Day is a day for reflection.

Mr. Speaker, today we observe International Women's Day, a day which marks the celebration of women's rights, and honours our contribution.
For so long, women's needs and concerns were ignored and excluded from processes of government. It was only 56 years ago that women were recognized as persons under the BNA Act, and the right to vote was granted only nine years earlier. Discrimination still exists in many areas, subtle, often as a result of attitudes.
In the Speech from the Throne our new Government outlined measures aimed at redressing economic and social inequalities faced by women in our country. I am proud to say that we have made substantial progress in addressing these concerns, through amendments regarding spouses allowances, removing the discrimination against Indian women, and with the statements to be made later today on the Abella Report. In this session we anticipate changes to the Divorce Act and the establishment of a parliamentary task force on child care. These are all issues of special though not exclusive concern to women.
We know other social change must occur before women achieve full equality not only in the eyes of the law but in the councils of those who hold power in business, government, and labour.
This morning my 15-year old son said to me: "Mom, why do we have a women's day? I bet we don't have a men's day". I would like to be able to answer him within the next decade-
I regret to advise the Hon. Member that her time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, the concept of International Women's Day was first advocated on March 8, 1910, when Socialist International held a conference commemorating the strike by New York women textile workers who, on March 8, 1857, began a labour struggle to improve their working conditions. Women's Day recalls the participation of women in an event unmistakably defined as a clear intent to redress injustices experienced on the labour scene. Today, once again the emphasis is on the economic independence sought by women for years.
Men and women alike are concerned about efforts aimed at making people more aware and promoting justice and equity in our society.
With respect to the status of women, 1985 will be just as significant as 1975 if only because next July will signal the end of the Decade for Women. Women have not achieved all their objectives, but their courage, determination and efforts to stir people have given rise to a new mentality which nurtures our aspirations towards justice and equality.
Initiatives should be undertaken in order to protect our aging population, preserve future generations, and ensure employment equity.
Today we reach out to women across the world and assure them of our support in their efforts-
I must advise the Hon. Member that her time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government has eliminated the energy division at the National Research Council. The energy division sponsored research and development of renewable energy resources, 70 per cent of which was contracted out to the private sector. It is estimated that some 2,000 small businesses will be drastically affected by the withdrawal of research and development assistance, and that approximately 15,000 jobs will be lost. Per million dollars, invested in alternate energy, twice as many jobs are created as in fossil fuel and nuclear energy projects.
The New Democratic Party is not only concerned about this job loss, but also about the fact that the Government is so short-sighted regarding the potential for Canada's renewable


March 8, 1985

energy industry on the international market. It is estimated that international sales in renewable energy, including solar, will increase from $3.5 billion in 1985 to $14.75 billion by 1990. Canada now has a fledgling solar industry which exported $4 million in photovoltaic products in 1984. Most of the products exported were developed under the guidance of the National Research Council's energy division. Technologies such as the "light pipe" super window, and photovoltaic water pumps, show considerable promise and are in high demand in developing nations around the world. This is in contrast to the CANDU reactor which is in demand nowhere.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR POLITICAL MECHANISMS TO CORRECT INJUSTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we are celebrating International Women's Day. Throughout the country, women are gathering to show their solidarity and to reflect on the themes of our major demands.
The women of Argenteuil-Papineau learned long ago to consult with each other and to solve problems together. I would like to pay tribute to their ongoing efforts in this respect.
Mr. Speaker, since women got the vote, a great deal of progress has been made. However, the fact remains that we are too often obliged to use in conjunction with the concept "rights", the terms "demands", "struggle" and "women". Mr. Speaker, it is also a fact that issues as basic as equal pay, abortion, maternity leave, day care centres, old age pensions, shelters for battered women, rape legislation and sexual har-rassment are still the subject of public debate in 1985.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to see all women make this a day of increased awareness of the status of women here and in other countries, in countries where women are hungry, cold and afraid. Let us hope that this 33rd Parliament will give us the political instruments we need to correct these inequities.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to give hearty congratulations to another woman,
Oral Questions
the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier). Her initiatives in waging war on acid rain put Canada on the cutting edge of environmental protection throughout the world. This Government has attained heights in its first six months that the former government failed to achieve in 16 years.
Canadian automobiles and light trucks will be equipped with emission standards equal to the United States, effective in 1988. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) must also be given credit for his wisdom in endorsing this necessary and vital measure. For the first time in the history of this country, we have some bargaining power to seek cut-backs in the United States.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) meets with President Reagan in Quebec City on March 17 and 18, he will take with him a new mandate supported by every Canadian who fears for our fragile environment. We will reduce sulphur dioxide emissions by 50 per cent by 1994. We will provide $150 million for emission controls at smelters. We will assure $25 million is used for technological development. We will investigate increased use of low sulphur coal from western Canada. We will organize an acid rain office to co-ordinate new policy.
I advocate the reconstitution of the federal sub-committee on acid rain to monitor the progress of this war we are waging. There will be many battles before the war is won-

Mr. Speaker, we don't seem to have much of a front bench. I see the Minister of Finance is not here.
Speak for yourself.
The Prime Minister is not here. I see the President of the Treasury Board is arriving.
What about your front bench?

Mr. Speaker, we are not the Government, and we expect the Government to be present. I must say that I am a little surprised, in view of the economic circumstances and the escalation in interest rates which we saw yesterday, that we do not have the Minister of Finance in the House. I will direct my question to the Deputy Prime Minister.

March 8, 1985
Oral Questions
We have seen the bank rate rise to just under 12 per cent. The Minister of Finance has constantly and repeatedly said that this is a temporary matter, and "wait until March". Well, we are in March.
Yes, the ides of March.

The trend is clear. We have had six consecutive weeks of interest rate increase, and the Government steadfastly refuses to act. We have the impression that this is a Government of handwringers, that the Ministers are out there wringing their hands. That is not what Canadians thought they elected back in September of last year. The economic summit is not necessary to tel! us that increasing interest rates are the most serious problem facing the economy of the country. I plead with the Government, through the Deputy Prime Minister, on behalf of home owners, farmers, fishermen, the unemployed, and small businesses, to use his good offices to ensure that action is taken immediately to stop the escalation in interest rates.

Mr. Speaker, the last time I wrung my hands was when the former Finance Minister in the Liberal Government brought down his Budget.
I should like to point out to the Hon. Member that this morning we have a modest recovery in the Canadian dollar and that we have some better news on the unemployment front because the people of the country have confidence in the Government. We will see the change in interest rates for which we are all hoping.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that the Minister of State for Finance is here. I wish they were wringing their hands, because at least they would be doing something. In fact I believe they are probably wringing their hands.

Mr. Speaker, a year ago on March 20, the present Minister of Finance asked my colleague at the time, the Hon. Marc Lalonde, some questions. He said, and I quote:
Will the Minister, on the strength of his convictions, stand up and offer his resignation if the Government's policies do not stem the slide in the Canadian dollar which today hit an 18-month low of 78.06 and was only stopped by massive intervention on the part of the Government?
I would therefore put the same question to the Minister of State (Finance). If a year ago, the resignation of Mr. Lalonde would have been appropriate, does the Minister of State believe, considering the economic situation in this country and the lack of confidence shown by the Prime Minister, that the Minister of Finance ought to offer his resignation?

Mr. Speaker, perhaps if Mr. Lalonde had resigned we
wouldn't be in as big a mess as we were when we took over the Government.
The Minister of Finance has the confidence of the Canadian people. He has expressed, in the House many times, his concern over interest rates. None of us like rising interest rates. We have reflected to the other side of the House that the strength in the U.S. dollar has been unique and has affected the currencies of all western nations, including Canada. The interest rate policy of the Bank has been to pursue a moderate, stabilizing influence.

Mr. Speaker, would the Minister of State for Finance tell us in concrete terms what advice she would offer the home owner whose mortgage is coming up for renewal, and the small-businessman who is basically labouring under increasing interest rates every day and is afraid to make capital investments?
I am not satisfied to stand here and hear this nonsense about last year, when we had one of the strongest growth records, delivered by a Liberal Government, of 4.7 per cent, and the lowest inflation rate of 3.7 per cent, better than the United States. What advice does the Minister have today to offer those people who are suffering every single day and who are not able to plan their future because of these escalating interest rates?

Mr. Speaker, Canadians have expressed their confidence in the future. Small business with which we have been discussing many of our policies, has expressed its support for what we are doing about bringing down the deficit. The best thing we can do for Canadians is return an atmosphere of confidence, which we are seeing all over the country.

subsubtopic: UNITED STATES STRATEGIC DEFENCE INITIATIVE-CANADIAN POSITION

Mr. Speaker, I would like to pose a question to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence. Yesterday we heard a plea from the Secretary-General of the United Nations that Canadians not become captive to the new nuclear technology. Today we are honouring International Women's Day. We know that no cause unites Canadian women more than their plea that Canada not contribute further to the arms race. In the spirit of those messages, I would ask the Minister of National Defence whether he thinks it is now time for the Government to reconsider its support for the U.S. star wars initiative.
March 8, 1985

In particular, because of a further apprehension raised by Mr. Nitze in Ottawa two days ago about the linkage between the radar agreement and star wars, will the Minister agree that no signing of any agreement should take place until there has been a thorough review by Members of this Parliament? Can he give us an assurance that the Government will not sign an agreement until Parliament has fully examined the conditions of that agreement?

He has just indicated that there is no link at all between the star wars concept, the policy of the American administration. He has indicated that the U.S. Government has specifically denied this connection.
Not many days ago Mr. Paul Nitze, a senior official of the American Government, while in this city, said that it remains to be seen, and prior to that the U.S. Secretary of Defense said that the updating of the DEW line is an integral part of the backup system for the star wars concept. How does the Deputy Prime Minister square these two statements, which do make a connection between the modernization of the DEW line and the star wars project, with the statement put out by the U.S. embassy yesterday or the day before?

March 8, 1985

Mr. Speaker, they are entirely consistent. I will show the Hon. Member, who obviously has not read a copy of this press release put out yesterday, the only inconsistency it contains. The only confusion or misconception is in the minds of the members of the Opposition and, I am afraid, also in the media. There is no linkage to the future of the SDI system. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that repeatedly, and we have a press release here which sets that out very clearly. The press release goes on to indicate:
We believe that these reports have been misleading. In responding to a hypothetical question, in Ottawa yesterday, Ambassador Nitze was merely pointing out that the President's Strategic Defence Initiative is a research project and that it is impossible at this time to predict what decisions will or will not be made at a considerably later date on any actual development or deployment.

Mr. Speaker, it is a research project that the U.S. Secretary of Defence has said involves an inextricable link with the modernization of the DEW line. I do not care what was said yesterday. There is a conflict between what was said yesterday by the U.S. Government and what the U.S. Secretary of Defense said. We on this side of the House want clarification of that.
If the Deputy Prime Minister is so certain that there is no connection, I would ask him, in the name of democracy, and because of the seriousness of the issue, why the Government does not bring a proposed treaty before the House of Commons for debate and discussion before it is signed by the two Governments.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, today is a landmark for this Government and indeed for all Canadians. Today we are taking a major step: we are opening doors to opportunities and to equality in the workplace.
Hear, hear!

I am sure that Members of the House will know of my long-standing commitment to equality. They will know that I have long dedicated my energies to the issues that I address today.

That is why I have the rare privilege of rising in the House to announce the measures this Government will take in response to the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Equality in Employment.

In her report which I tabled in November, Judge Rosalie Abella coined the phrase "employment equity". That phrase is short and simple but it singularly expresses the goal of this Government in promoting equal opportunities for women, for native people, for disabled persons and visible minorities- promoting equity in the workplace.
There are some plain facts that face us in this country today. It is a fact that women, on average, earn only 64 cents for every dollar earned by men. Fully 77 per cent of women are found in only five of the 22 major job categories, those at the bottom of the salary scale. It is a fact that the recently released study Who Gets The Work pointed out that "whites have three job prospects for every one for blacks". Fact: among employable disabled persons, 50 per cent are unemployed. Fact: in many native communities unemployment is higher than 70 per cent.
As a country, we cannot afford to exclude these Canadians from full participation in the workplace. We need their contribution to the economic renewal and the growth of this country. In the past, lip service has been paid to the concept of equality in the workplace. It has been talked about, studied and worried about. What we need is action. That is what I am announcing today.
This Government will require Crown corporations, federally regulated businesses and contractors providing goods and services to the federal Government to implement employment equity. Crown corporations will be required to report annually to Parliament on their plans and progress, beginning in 1986. Federally regulated businesses with 100 or more employees will be required by legislation to report annually to Parliament on their plans and progress with a three-year phasing in period to establish the necessary information and data systems.
March 8, 1985

Businesses seeking Government contracts for goods and services of $200,000 or more will have to show their compliance or stand to lose their right to compete for government business.

The approach we have chosen will enable companies to develop plans compatible with their individual needs. There will be no major administrative costs or unnecessary and heavy-handed intervention.

We are not creating a massive bureaucratic enforcement agency and we will not impose an unwieldy set of rigid procedures. Instead, we will draw on the energies and inventiveness of employers in removing barriers that now stand across the path of visible minorities, of women, disabled persons and native people. The means are flexible but the goal is fixed: employment equity.

Mr. Speaker, for the first time, disclosure of the results obtained will be compulsory. For the first time, all information will be made public. Public scrutiny will be a precious tool since it will provide an incentive for obtaining genuine and tangible results.

With this information in hand, the powers and authorities of the Human Rights Commission can be properly exercised. When action is needed to ensure equity in the workplace, action will be taken.
The Government will be discussing these measures in the next few weeks with representatives of visible minorities, business, women, disabled persons, labour and native people. We will be telling them, as I am informing the House today, that this Government is committed to action and that we expect results.
Hear, hear!

Equally important, we will be seeking their views on legislative measures to be introduced into the House by June of this year.
With regard to equal pay for work of equal value, the Government must first set its own house in order and this has not been done. We are committed to doing so. To that end my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), is inviting the Pubic Service unions to join us in developing an implementation plan for equal pay for work of equal value. I understand that he expects their preliminary report by June 30 of this year.
In total, the measures I have announced today will touch the working environment of over one million Canadians. This is a first and major step but I do emphasize that it is only the first step. We will not be satisfied until the goal-the concept of fair access and equal opportunities for advancement-is a reality from coast to coast, from the shipyard to the assembly line, to the corporate boardroom. We will remove the barriers
Employment
that restrict the economic future of so many Canadians. Our economic development, the development of this country, depends on and demands the full participation of all. Give Canadians real opportunities and they will get the jobs. Give them the jobs and they will create wealth. Generate wealth and there will be economic growth, and economic growth will develop more jobs.
[ Translation]
Jobs in all sectors of industry, in companies large and small. I would like to add at this point that small- and medium-sized businesses will not be obliged to comply with the measures announced today. However, we are confident that they too will implement employment equity measures since they are also anxious to reap the benefits of increased productivity.

The few people in business, Sir, who indeed have already adopted employment equity have told me that they have seen substantial growth in their productivity, in their profits and most importantly in their people. The value of investment, not just in plants and machinery but in people, was clearly recognized at the First Ministers' conference in Regina. There we embarked on an entirely new approach to labour market development. Fundamental to the new direction that was taken at that time is equity. Fair access for all Canadians to new training and new employment opportunities. This strategy will tackle head on the problem of trapping minorities in employment ghettoes. We will tackle head on the critical problem of job re-entry for women.
The measures I am announcing today in response to the Abella report will join those efforts announced earlier in a comprehensive attack on barriers to equity in the workplace. These measures are a major step forward in the progress of economic renewal. More than that, this is a step forward in the pursuit of economic justice. It is a step that will help to ensure that the benefits of growth and renewal will be shared by all Canadians.
Hear, hear!
This is another step toward a better future for Canada, a future of opportunity, a future of equal opportunity.

Hear, hear!

Dirty pool.

The Government talks about wanting to have better debates in this House, yet the Government did not deliver the document, the basis of the debate, until Question Period had started and we were occupied with other things.
Shame!
Where were you this morning-
I was here, Mr. Speaker.
Where were you this morning when we wanted unanimous consent?

We would not give that unanimous consent because the Government did not produce the document that was to be discussed.
Worse still-and I want to give you notice, Mr. Speaker, of a question of privilege-this document was delivered to the press before it was delivered to Members of Parliament. I checked that. The Government could get the document to the press but the Government could not get the document to Members of Parliament.
That is trampling on Parliament.

That is the real attitude the Government has to Parliament. The rest is rhetoric and media politics. That is all we get out of that Government.
With respect to the statement, we cannot, as I said, give the subject matter the attention it should have at this time. There are, however, some forward steps in the statement. We are pleased for those forward steps. They are the fruition of what was begun by the former Liberal Government in passing the Human Rights Act, sometimes against opposition on the other side, and in bringing in the Charter of Rights, in particular the equality sections that will go into effect on April 17.
When the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) appointed Judge Abella to carry out this commission, the initiative was indicative of the Goverment of Canada's commitment to increase the employability and productivity of disadvantaged groups. The commission of inquiry was to
examine and report on ways to assist women, native people, disabled individuals and visible minorities to compete on an equal basis for employment opportunities. The Member also stated on that occasion that the elimination of systemic discrimination is essential to ensure that there is full participation of all Canadians in the public and private sectors. The growth of the Canadian economy depends on such participation. That was when the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry appointed Judge Abella to carry out that commission on July 27, 1983.

I have read the statement quickly. Some parts are vague and will need much clarification. We will be asking for some clarification this morning during the question period that follows.
One of the main points that Judge Abella makes in her report was that voluntary action was not working and we needed legislation.
Let us examine what the Minister has announced. She says that Crown corporations will be required to report annually to Parliament on their plans and progress beginning in 1986. But in another document which the Minister of Employment and Immigration gave us at the last minute, she says there will be no legislation.
We don't need legislation.

I am interested in knowing how the Minister intends to oblige the Crown corporations to do what she wants them to do. I would like to know what the sanctions are, and why she did not bring in legislation such as Judge Abella had recommended. In addition, Judge Abella recommended that this reporting apply to Crown corporations and federal agencies. There is no mention of the federal agencies in the Minister's statement.
With respect to federally-regulated business, and this includes Bell Telephone, Canadian Pacific Railway, the companies that come under the federal Goverment's jurisdiction for labour purposes, the Minister says that federally-regulated businesses with 100 or more employees will be required, in this case by legislation, to report annually to Parliament on their plans and progress with a three-year phasing in period.
The Minister says elsewhere that this applies only to 800 out of 4,500 companies. There is no explanation. We would want to know why only 800. I would also want to know what the sanctions are if the wishes ofthe Government are not adhered to.
With respect to contract compliance, the Minister says that businesses seeking government contracts for goods and services of $200,000 or more will have to show their compliance or stand to lose their right to compete for government business. Again, I am interested as to whether there will be legislation or will it be done by administrative action? The Minister said

it would only apply to 100 companies. Members opposite are laughing; they do not pay much attention to Judge Abella. They should read the report. Judge Abella said that legislation was required. Employment
We have had a statement this morning on the Government's response to the Abella report. My first reaction has to be that the Government has stolen the words of Judge Abella but not the substance of the report. The Government across the way has a mandate to act or enforce what Judge Abella is saying, but I think it has chosen not to act in a substantive way. If the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had said that it should be done in the federal Government, Crown corporations and the private sector, with his mandate we could have employment equity, we could have equal pay for work of equal value, we could have all the things about which Judge Abella talked in her report.

As I said in English, they have stolen the words of Judge Abella, but they completely forgot the practical aspects of the report.

The first thing is employment equity. We find in the Government's statement this morning that there is no enforcement, outside of a voluntary appeal and lots of good words that there should be employment equity in the country. It is one thing to have rhetoric but it is another thing to have some real enforcement for the women and the minorities to whom the report refers-the visible minorities, the native people of Canada and the disabled. I ask the Minister and the Government: Where are the goals in her statement for employment equity? Where are the targets in her statement for employment equity? Where is the timetable in terms of imposing employment equity? Where are the sanctions? How can we have something without sanctions? Where is the enforcement mechanism? In the report of Judge Abella three or four different ways were outlined to enforce employment equity. Where are the enforcement mechanisms which are so necessary for this to work?
When it comes to enforcement, Judge Abella said that the voluntary mechanisms would not work and that we needed a mandatory mechanism. On page 195 of the report the following appears:
A voluntary program which a mandatory reporting requirement is nonetheless voluntary in the absence of a requirement to remedy the discriminatory practices disclosed by the information reported.
A requirement of public reporting may result in public pressure on a company to revise its systems but it is unrealistic to rely on public opinion as an effective monitoring agent. It results in a speculative and scattered approach and creates the perception, in the absence of enforcement, that the issue is deserving of only casual attention.
If we are to have employment equity in the country, we need an enforcement mechanism to ensure that it occurs. We have had a lot of good will and good words in the past. People have said that we could do this in a voluntary sense, but it just has not happened. This is why we need some enforcement.
As I said before, the Minister has stolen the words of Judge Abella, not the substance of her report. Also the Minister mentioned in her statement the importance of publishing information, making public all kinds of information. That in itself is not enough.

March 8, 1985
Employment
[ Translation]
We, in this country, have often looked into the situation of Canadian women, native women, visible minorities and the handicapped, with much publicity throughout the land. Judge Abella has produced a good report with many recommendations, and I agree with most of the recommendations denouncing inequality, inequity towards Canadian women, the handicapped, native people or other visible minorities here in Canada.
But what we need now, Mr. Speaker, is action. The time has come to do something in Canada. The Minister borrowed the words of Judge Abella, Mr. Speaker, but she forgot the practical aspects of the judge's report.

The fourth point I want to make this morning concerns the whole question of equal pay for work of equal value. In her statement this morning the Minister talked about the dismal record of the country in this particular area. Of course, I agree with her. I think we should look at her statement very carefully. She refers to the federal Government only, that she wants to rectify this situation in the Public Service. There is a bit of a timetable in her statement. The Government will enter into a consultative process to bring about the whole principle of equal pay for work of equal value. However, there is nothing in her statement for Crown corporations. There is nothing at all pertaining to the private sector when it comes to this very important question. There is nothing at all when it comes to government purchasing, and the Government purchased several billions of dollars worth of goods and services every year.
It is fine to apply the principle only to the federal Public Service, but what about the other areas that are so important? The Government has an important mandate. If the Prime Minister gives the word, I am sure he would have co-operation to implement the principle of equal pay for work of equal value, not only in the Public Service but in Crown corporations, in government purchasing and in the private sector. I suggest to the Minister that the Government should act according to that principle and sentiment.
As the Minister has said, there is tremendous discrimination against visible minorities in the country, such as black Canadians who are faced with real difficulties, as we discovered the other night in Toronto, finding jobs as compared with white Canadians. Also we find that about 50 per cent of the employable disabled people and 70 per cent or more of Indian and Metis people are without jobs. Because those figures are so harsh and real, the Minister should apply the principle across the board. We need more than just words and rhetoric; we must apply the principles which Judge Abella recommended in her report.
In the last while the action group of my Party met with disabled Canadians. There was a very moving example in Halifax about a month ago when we were told by an organization of disabled Canadians about the need for contract compliance, affirmative action and employment equity for disabled Canaians. We were told that disabled Canadians tended to be
the forgotten people in our country and were discriminated against greatly when seeking jobs.
The Minister did not deal adequately in her statement this morning with the question of government purchasing. In this area she is being very timid and is taking a Mickey Mouse approach. She says the government purchasing section applies to around a hundred companies in the country. Judge Abella says in her report at page 227 that in 1980 the Canadian Government purchased goods and services from between 25,000 and 30,000 companies, worth $6.5 billion to the private sector, and an additional $5.5 billion worth went to Crown corporations. That was around $12 billion back in 1980. As I say, there are between 25,000 and 30,000 companies involved, and all this compliance will apply to is the 100 largest companies in this country. She could be a lot more bold than that.
[ Translation]
There is another important point, Mr. Speaker, and that is training. In Regina two or three weeks ago, and I was there with the Minister for the First Ministers' Conference, the Minister announced a training program for Canadians which unfortunately allocated only 17 per cent of its funding for Canadian women and Canadian youth. Funding for other groups mentioned in the Abella Report was not very generous either, and I am thinking of native people, visible minorities and the disabled.

Once again that is an example where the Minister is very long on rhetoric but very short when it comes to substance.
Another area is the whole question of child care. Yesterday this Party had an opportunity to meet with about 15 or 16 women's groups from across the country here in Ottawa. One thing they mentioned time and time again was that if we are to have equality and equity for the women of Canada, we must provide adequate day care and child care services. We heard from the Prime Minister during the campaign the promise to put a lot more dollars into child care in Canada. What have we had since? We only have the promise of another study. We tend to study, study, study. I say to the Minister that the time for study is rapidly ending and the time for action is now approaching. We have a comprehensive study and a lot of specific recommendations. How about implementing some of those recommendations on child care?
We can have employment equity in this country. We can have employment equity for the four groups mentioned in this report. We can have employment equity just as we have employment equity now for Francophones in the Public Service.
[ Translation]
And I agree with this affirmative action program for Francophone women, and I am sure all Parties in the House will agree, Mr. Speaker, but we could do exactly the same thing for the other groups mentioned in this report.
March 8, 1985



We must, as I said before, have enforcement. Without enforcement, we are not going to have any action at all, or very little. In the United States, where there are some mandatory laws, it has been found, first, that it improves equality for minority groups and improves equality for women; and, second, it has made those particular industries more productive in the United States. I suggest that the same wouldhappen in the country.
We can and must have goals, targets, opportunity and more money for training and child care. In conclusion, we must give the people of this country an opportunity. We must give them equality. We must give them the tools to build a new country, a new vision for Canada where everybody will be put back to work and we will become a nation of producers. Putting Canada back to work will mean more fairness for every Canadian, more opportunities for every Canadian, more fairness for one and all.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister.
The Abella Report contains at least fifty recommendations on training, especially language training for immigrants and for women who work in the home. I wonder whether, considering the Abella Report's recommendations, the Minister could negotiate new agreements with the provinces on second language teaching, either French or English, for courses for women working in the home which would of course require some financial arrangement for babysitters, in any case for the whole language training issue. Mrs. Abella mentions the subject in at least fifty recommendations. I wonder whether the Minister could give us her views on the subject today and let us know where the Government is going and whether she intends to introduce a definitive policy, with the co-operation of the provinces, for setting up these language training programs.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) for his question. A number of recommendations have been made in the Abella report with regard to Vinformation, the training area. These have all been taken into the ongoing review-and Regina was the first step of it-of training and job creation being conducted by my Department. Some of that will have to be developed with regard to training for native people, for example, with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie). There will be other areas which touch directly on programs relating to the Secretary of State (Mr. McLean), and this will be developed with him. The fact is that the whole thrust of training as agreed to at Regina is being worked out now on a federal-provincial basis. One thing that impressed me
Employment
in Regina was the fact that there was co-operation in this field by the First Ministers of the provinces. I look forward to seeing that continued.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister why she has not dealt with the whole question of part-time work. As she knows only too well, the large majority of part-time workers, some 72 per cent a couple of years ago, are women. We recently found that Crown corporations, Air Canada being the prime example, are trying to press for unlimited part-time jobs in their contracts. This will be targeted particularly at women. Women who have been employed full-time will be forced into part-time jobs without adequate benefits. They will not have adequate chance for all kinds of opportunities, for example, job improvement and training, such as they would have with a full-time job. Why are part-time workers not mentioned? This is vital. What is she going to do about part-time workers as far as employment equity is concerned?

Mr. Speaker, there is no exclusion of part-time workers from this report. The approach that has been taken is looking at ways in which Crown corporations, federally-regulated businesses and those businesses having contract compliance will develop their employment equity plans to meet their needs. That includes part-time workers. It does not exclude them. I want the Hon. Member to know that.
I would also like the Hon. Member to recognize that in the agreements that were arrived at in Regina she may have noticed that there was one area where the federal Government committed something in the vicinity of $100 million for innovation. That is an area where I hope progress can be made with regard to flexible work hours, part-time, child care structures, all of this.
We want full-time, not part-time.
The Hon. Member does not recognize that I mentioned flexible work hours and part-time workers. All of this will be dealt with in that field as well, but it will be interrelated.

Mr. Speaker, I would begin by congratulating the Minister on making the announcement in the House. I listened to the critic from the Liberal Party. I was critic on behalf of the Opposition for over four years. On one occasion and one occasion only was an announcement made in the House. The common practice was for me to have a good day when I could pick up the actual announcement within 24 hours after the announcement was made somewhere else in the country. The average was close to two days. So we are in good shape.
The thrust of what the Minister said in the House today is that we are going to get employment equity in this country that its sensitive to local communities, sensitive to local aims of government and their function, sensitive to local businesses and the functions they perform in the local community. Am I correct in drawing the conclusion that this is a program that

March 8, 1985
Employment
will be really sensitive to all the differences between communities and businesses in the country?

Mr. Speaker, not only this major step that we took today but the announcement that was made in Regina emphasized that the thrust of the Government will be toward recognizing local issues, local needs, regional disparities and regional differences. I know the critic for the New Democratic Party has said in the discussions he is having across the country with many of the people to whom I spoke that decentralization from Ottawa is definitely needed in this field. This would place more self-reliance on individuals, organizations and communities. That is the whole thrust of the Government's new labour market strategy and of today's announcement.
I should also tell the Hon. Member that in sending the preliminary material to the official critics of the opposition Parties, I was assured by both offices that it had arrived before Queston Period.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps one of the things to which the Minister can address herself is her concept of the purpose of Parliament and her idea of allowing an opportunity for people to debate the issues. What is the purpose of making a statement in the House of Commons when the Official Opposition has no chance to respond to that statement? Something of such moment and importance as the Abella report which deals with four very important groups about which this Parliament is concerned and wishes to give them their dignity and human rights is brought up on a Friday. I would think that this would be a matter of great importance to this Parliament.
Members of the Official Opposition had not been given notes or information about the statement until it had been made. The statement was brought before the press before it was brought before us. As the Opposition critic for issues affecting the handicapped and as the deputy critic for issues affecting minority groups and visible minorities, I feel that that is a deprivation of my opportunity to get the information 1 think I ought to have in order to be able to approach this question.
Come back tomorrow.

Tomorrow is Saturday. Members of the NDP should look at their calendars.
This issue is something which requires some concern.
Let's get at the issue.
Question.

There is a great deal of noise coming from my left side where Members of the NDP sit.
One of the promises that was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) during the election campaign was that he would in fact bring in those recommendations contained in
Sections 26 and 27 of the report entitled Obstacles. That report made recommendations that required legislation and compulsory action on the part of the Government-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I would ask the Hon. Member to put his question to the Minister, this being a question period. The Hon. Member's preamble has well exceeded the usual time allotted for the asking of a question. Would he please put the question to the Minister?

Mr. Speaker, the question is related to the promise made by the Prime Minister that the limit for government contracts would be $20,000. Unless the Minister made an error in reading her script, she seemed to indicate that the level at which a contract must be before there will be some concern on the part of the Government regarding asking a private sector organization to comply with these requirements will be $200,000. That seems to be 10 times the amount mentioned by the Prime Minister. Will the Minister be satisfied with this promise-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I now recognize the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald).

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member began by asking what I thought Parliament was for. I think it is for discussing issues such as this. That is why I have taken the time to make this statement in the House of Commons. That did not normally happen when the Liberal Government was in office.
Hear, hear!

As the Hon. Member perhaps heard, I have also announced that there will be legislation coming before Parliament on these issues. I would trust that he would be here to debate those issues and discuss and study this legislation when it goes to committee. I would also say that reports were sent to the employment critics of the House of Commons. I am the Minister of Employment and Immigration. I am not responsible for other areas. Therefore, I sent the announcement to the official critics.
The Hon. Member wanted to know about the $200,000 limit with regard to contract compliance. I can tell him that that affects 100 of the largest companies. In total, private companies do something in the vicinity of $6 billion worth of business in goods and services under government contracts. Those 100 companies to which contract compliance will apply do 75 per cent of that $6 billion worth of business. The great bulk of moneys that are dispensed by the Government to private companies will be covered by the steps being taken today.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). The Minister has expressed her commitment to employment equity and her concern about visible minorities. She knows that second-language training in English or French is crucial to visible minorities and recent immigrants so that they may
March 8, 1985

have adequate employment opportunities. I am wondering why the Minister, having expressed her concern about visible minorities and about equity, has made no announcement today regarding adequate funding for language training.

Mr. Speaker, that is because those issues were addressed in the over-all agreement that was arrived at in Regina. At that time we spoke about training as it applies to women, native people and visible minorities. I would like the Hon. Member to understand that the labour market strategy that was announced in Regina and the agreements that were reached with the provinces enable us for the first time to work together to meet the very concerns expressed by the Hon. Member. In that $900 million which is totally allocated for programs that will be worked out with the provinces and the private sector, training and second language will be a very major concern.
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to compliment the Minister. I am really very pleased.
Hear, hear!

On behalf of the Liberal Party, 1 would like to express the fact that I see this as a part of the ongoing steps of development started by one of the Minister's very good friends, Judy LaMarsh. I know that in the history of the development of equity, affirmative action and equality for women, it has been an uphill fight for all women regardless of political affiliation. I am really pleased to see this step being taken. I do, however, have questions. I must admit to the Minister that I did not receive a copy of the report so I cannot ask her the kinds of pointed questions that would elicit the responses I want.
My general gut feeling is that even with the Minister's desire to see this ongoing development continue in keeping with the Royal Commission on the Status of Women report which began in 1967, with the Advisory Council in 1973 and with many other events which I will not read into the record, I am really concerned about what I heard from the Minister. Does she believe that in not applying a mandatory requirement for reporting, the Canadian Human Rights Commission will not be given the kind of manpower and finances it needs? If it is not given to the Canadian Human Rights Commission, then to whom will it be given and how? She is creating goodwill no doubt, but how does she see the reporting so that we can supervise what she wants to accomplish for all women, visible minorities and the handicapped, some of whom are also women?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments which the Hon. Member made. She knows, as I do, of the ongoing struggle in taking steps and measures such as the ones which were announced today. We realize that struggle is there, but every time something moves forward, there are a great many of us who are that much more pleased. But we never give up the struggle.
Employment
Because the Hon. Member has not had an opportunity to read this document in detail, I will tell her that the reporting is mandatory. It is mandatory for Crown corporations and it is mandatory, by legislation, for federally-regulated businesses. As those reports are received on an annual basis, they will be tabled in Parliament and made public. Under its present legislation, the Canadian Human Rights Commission will be able to initiate action if it feels that the goals are not being met.

Mr. Speaker, I am very proud to see that after six months in power and only a few months after the Abella Report was published, the Progressive Conservative Government has now been able to table in the House some concrete measures on equality in the workplace.
The question I would like to put to the Minister, and which is of great concern to me, concerns maternity leave. I would like to know whether, in the near future, the next step will be to consider that women need supplementary maternity leave in addition to what they have now, in order to be able to raise and care for their young children more consistently and with let us say better results than is the case today. Does the Minister intend to consider this matter in the near future?
Mr. Speaker, when I was listening to the Hon. Member, I asked myself when was the last time a Government responded to a royal commission report within three months?
Hear, hear!
Some royal commission reports seldom get a response. The suggestions which the Hon. Member has made are very relevant and I will certainly give them consideration.
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to encourage the Government to continue making statements. I think it is a helpful process when it is done in the House.
Hear, hear!

The Minister will know that up to 20 per cent of the projected increase in the labour force, especially in the western provinces in the next decade, will involve native young people. What plans does the Minister have to increase, rather than decrease, pre-employment training programs and particularly life-skills training? What steps has she planned for following the recommendation of the report, that there be innovative mobile training centres, especially in northern and remote areas, to help those people prepare for the jobs which they need badly?

Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned earlier, the measures which have been announced today fit into the wider program of the new labour force strategy which was agreed

March 8, 1985
Employment
upon in Regina. I mentioned that because a number of provincial Governments, particularly the Government of the Province of Saskatchewan, raised the issue which was raised by the Hon. Member. In that sense, the thrust and directions which were decided upon in Regina will enable several target groups to have programs more effectively directed to them. The target group which is covered by the new programs, and job entry, will take young native people from the educational situation where they may be at the moment, and increase that educational opportunity to have it lead to work experience. Money has been allocated for that. At the present time we are working, together with the provinces and native people, to decide where and how these programs can best be allocated to the concerned regions. I can tell the Hon. Member, having arrived at the principles and an over-all agreement in Regina, that we are working on detailed plans for each of these programs.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that at least the rhetoric is there as far as it concerns the removal of barriers for re-entrance into the workforce, specifically as it affects women. I imagine the Minister had in mind the women who, for one reason or another, had to leave the workforce and are trying to return. It is very difficult for women to get back into the workforce, even when jobs are available. Women are discriminated against, especially in high unemployment areas. The greatest discriminator against those women is the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) because of her hiring guidelines which went to every single Manpower office in the country.
In view of the fine rhetoric today which indicated that the barriers would be removed, I would like to ask the Minister, for all the remaining direct job-creation projects that come under her jurisdiction which have not yet started but will start in the coming months, will she remove the restriction against hiring new entrants and re-entrants in the hiring criteria? Will she also tell the House if she will undertake to remove those same restrictions which, as she said, discriminate against women in the federal-provincial agreements which will be arrived at for direct job creation this coming fall? Yes or no? Or will she blame it on the Liberals?

Mr. Speaker, of course, that is very easy to do because the guidelines were set up by the former Government. I understand the importance of the steps which have been taken today. I waited 15 years for something like this. I sat in the House of Commons and urged the former Liberal Government to be much more assertive about affirmative action programs.
To address the question of job creation, it is because the job-creation projects of the past did not work for women, long-term unemployed and young people who were seeking entry into the labour force that we have developed a new labour force strategy. The Hon. Member does not seem to comprehend that. Indeed, we are making major changes in all of the programs. I am sorry, with the number of years he sat
on the government side, that he could not bring the Liberal Government to take some of these steps.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to congratulate the Minister. I think women on all sides of the House, and women across Canada, are heartened today by the model which the Minister has put forward.
Hear, hear!

I am also pleased to see such a reasonable approach. Some of the concerns which the small business community had, most of which businesses are headed by women, have been addressed. I am pleased to see the Minister's approach, particularly with respect to contract compliance.
Could the Minister share with us a few examples of the kind of assistance which she would anticipate being provided to companies under the contract compliance section, and the criteria by which their plans would be assessed?

Mr. Speaker, the guidelines and the techniques which will be agreed upon with companies, whether they are companies which purchase from the Government or companies which come under the federally-regulated sector, will be discussed with each company. There have already been guidelines developed which can be utilized.
I would like to give a few examples. The following list outlines examples of measures which employers could implement: on-the-job training for target group members; development of an inventory of qualified, competent and interested target group members; orientation regarding career planning; work site modified as appropriate for women and/or disabled persons; jobs being widely advertised using target group media to recruit; company to ensure that all selection criteria are valid; and there are a number of other measures. All of these will be discussed with these companies so that they can put into effect a fair and just employment equity plan. I would see that this is done as we come down to making sure that these companies have in place the necessary systems for reporting the data and information which will be required.
