Mr. Speaker, I will do my best to turn this well-phrased question into a comment.
I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Skeena on his participation in Wednesday's debate. It was a good deal more positive than I expected it to be, quite frankly. One of the benefits of interrupting a Member midspeech is that other Members have time to compose comments like this.
March 8, 1985

The Member for Skeena made the point that the powers given to the Minister to manage the fishery for a wide variety of purposes are absolutely essential. At page 2806 of Hansard he spoke of:
-the very delicate dilemma this country would find itself in if it was impossible for different Ministries... to manage the resource for social or economic reasons.
While he supports the Bill, he did make some suggestions. He asked about the implications of Section 2.1(d) of the "purposes" section, which reads:
-to provide, in cooperation with the provinces, for the proper management, allocation and control of the inland fisheries of Canada.
He wants to know why we are bringing the provinces in. It is no mystery.
In the inland fisheries in general, the right to fish comes under provincial jurisdiction. We cannot undertake to allocate provincial property, so we added the qualifying phrase to avoid any suggestion of intrusion on existing indisputable provincial rights.
My comment concerns the Hon. Member's objection to the amendment to paragraph 34(m) of the Act. The amended paragraph would permit the enactment of regulations:
-authorizing a person engaged or employed in the administration or enforcement of this Act to vary, in respect of any area or portion thereof, any close time, fishing quota or limit on the size or weight of fish that has been fixed by the regulations.
He says that this power is beyond anything anyone in the House has yet imagined. However, has he read the existing legislation? Does he realize that we are just adding two refinements to the existing on-site powers delegated to fishery officers? Fishery managers already can be empowered to vary close times for entire management areas. By adding the words "in respect of any area or portion thereof', we merely allow exercise of that power over a small geographical area, over portions of management areas. Does the Member realize that this is the impact of the legislation?
I should explain that the addition of the power to vary size or weight limits is simply an alternative management tool to opening or closing an area. It is a refinement of existing practices.
I hope the Hon. Member will also realize that granting these on-site powers to fisheries officers in respect of sub-areas will allow fishermen greater fishing opportunities. It will give fishermen access to selected fishing grounds in parts of the management area that cannot be opened in its entirety because it would endanger the stocks. This power would allow the fishery manager right there on the spot to close off the particular limited area where the endangered stocks are, while leaving the rest of the area open for fishing.
Does the Hon. Member prefer the existing blunt instrument of opening or closing entire large management areas? Does he want these decisions taken quickly and effectively on-site or does he want to preserve the current lengthy process of enactment by order in council?
Fisheries Act

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's intervention is perhaps a good place to start. He said that the Government did not want to infringe upon provincial jurisdiction and there would be a consultative process. Any infringement upon provincial jurisdiction is really subject to an interpretation of the courts. The same is true with respect to infringement upon federal jurisdiction.
For example, with respect to infringement of rights, it is quite possible for a court judge to interpret these amendments, once they are enacted, as being an infringement upon provincial jurisdiction. The first amendment, 1(a), is to include "portions of fish" under the definition of fish. That is a new section of the Act. The explanatory notes say that portions of fish would allow control in management of fish which has been processed to some degree; for example, headed, gutted or filleted fish.
It is a well known article of law that once fish are captured they become real property. We also know that according to the Constitution, provincial jurisdiction comes under property and civil rights. Once a fish is captured it becomes real property. Therefore, it could eventually be interpreted by a court judge that this section cannot be implemented under the Fisheries Act.
Let us look at the clause in terms of the Hon. Member's comment about not wanting to infringe on provincial jurisdiction. Clause 1(b) includes in the definition of fish marine plants and portions thereof. The explanatory notes say that marine plants were formerly not included in the definition of fish. Anything attached to the seabed from headland to headland-in fact, out to three miles in some provinces-is provincial jurisdiction according to the interpretation of the courts.
In other words, as a result of decisions made by Supreme Court judges in the past, a provincial Government could not only control what is attached to the immediate seabed in every bay and cove on the East Coast of Canada, it could also be interpreted to mean under that law that the provincial Government could issue lobster licences because lobsters are on the seabed. If a net were attached to the seabed, then that could be interpreted to mean provincial jurisdiction.
These issues have been discussed between ministers in provincial jurisdictions. However, they do not issue lobster licences or licences for nets that are attached to the seabeds in their bays and coves because they know that according to federal law the federal Government has the rights to open and close seasons and limit the extent of that season for protection and conservation purposes. There would be no purpose for a provincial Government to issue lobster licences because the federal Government, under federal law, would have to shorten the fishing time.
The two additions to the Act which we are debating today could be perceived by a court judge to be an infringement upon provincial jurisdiction. This is not to say they should not be in the Act because we have seen provincial laws enacted that are really an infringement upon federal jurisdiction. I recall a couple of years ago the Province of Nova Scotia enacted a law that unilaterally seized control of the continental
March 8, 1985

Fisheries Act
shelf off the coast of the Province of Nova Scotia, and the wording went "and extensions thereof'; and the wording further went "to the extent of exploitability".
The drafter of that Bill in the Nova Scotia legislature took that section out of some charter of the mid-50s in Europe when there was an International Law of the Sea meeting. "To the extent of exploitability" meant as far as the technology would carry a drill ship, or whatever the case is, for the purpose of drilling for oil. In 1980 terms "to the extent of exploitability", meant you could drill an oil well in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. By passing a law in a legislative jurisdiction, you are passing it for a purpose, but although it is on the books, it does not really mean anything. If you went by the Nova Scotia law, "and extensions thereof' and "to the extent of exploitability" mean right across the Atlantic Ocean. If somebody walked out in the water off the coast of Africa, he could be charged with trespassing on Nova Scotia soil. It operates both ways in response to the hon. gentleman's question. Look at the ongoing disputes between provincial and federal Governments.
I have with me today a recent discussion paper passed to this new federal Government, the Mulroney Government as it is commonly known outside this Chamber, on behalf of the provincial Government of Newfoundland, by the Hon. A. Brian Peckford. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) should know this. I notice his Parliamentary Secretary is here. I only wish the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) were here. The Premier on behalf of the Newfoundland Government says in this paper delivered to the new Conservative Government:
Newfoundland believes that it must have a prominent role and in certain cases the paramount voice in the management of the fisheries resource in those areas which are adjacent to the province.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the Newfoundland Government wants a prominent role to manage the fishery off the coast of Newfoundland. The Premier does not stop there. He said that to achieve this goal "we have proposed a constitutional amendment to the federal Government".
I wonder what the response to that will be from the federal Minister of Fisheries. The Premier of Newfoundland goes on on behalf of his Government to say that in particular, resource allocation policy-which is what we are talking about in this Bill-for the northern cod way out in the Atlantic Ocean, hundreds of miles north of Newfoundland and east of Labrador, must grant priority access to the Newfoundland inshore fleet. In other words, toward the east, the north, the northeast coast of Newfoundland, out into the ocean, the Premier says first priority must be granted to the Newfoundland fleet.
Then he says that the second priority for access to this stock should be Newfoundland offshore vessels which land their catch at resource-short seasonal plants in communities adjacent to the stock. That is a further division, Mr. Speaker.
Then the Premier says that the third priority is for the remainder of the offshore fleet based in Newfoundland, and the fourth priority is for the Maritime Provinces respectively.
It would be interesting in this great time of consultation and of trying to appease the wishes of the provinces to find out what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) thinks of the Premier of Newfoundland's submission to him, given to him since he was elected. I bring this up because it is relevant to this Bill before us today. You get to the actual purpose of the Bill when you get to the section that outlines the purposes under this new Act.
An interesting question has been raised here. Right now according to the justice who made this decision in the court in British Columbia-and I would say that justice was absolutely correct in the decision that he made-the federal Government does not have the right to distinguish between gear types. It has been illegal all the way along for the federal Government to say in the case of a salmon fishery or a herring fishery: "All right, the big boats can have x amount of fish; the small inshore boats can have x amount of fish. That was always illegal but it was never tested properly in the courts.
The case presented before the federal Government said that we should have this power because there are the small boat fishermen or another group of fishermen who are really not getting enough fish to keep themselves alive. Therefore, we have a social and an economic responsibility toward fishermen. Nowhere in the present Act does it outline that the federal Department of Fisheries has a social and economic responsibility toward fishermen. Why, Mr. Speaker? Because that problem was never supposed to occur. In other words, it was not historically the duty of the federal Government to look at the socio-economic breakdown within the fishery and make resource allocations accordingly. It was not necessary. All of a sudden it is necessary. It has been necessary for the last eight to ten years. It is necessary because we have not, as the Government of Canada, devoted enough money toward research. We have not devoted enough money and now we have the recent cuts introduced by this Government into this Parliament which are laying off research people right across the country in fisheries, closing down research stations and cancelling expansions to research stations. These cuts are aggravating the problem. The duty of the Department of Fisheries now will become a socio-economic problem.
If you are going to get into that territory, Mr. Speaker, then you had better do it all and have a policy that says: "All right, what happens to the fish once it is landed? That is within provincial jurisdiction, but we have a socio-economic responsibility. Let's can the fish. Let's make sure it is going to the best use". Then you really get into it because of the waste that happens in the fishery today.
Let me outline what happens to capelin that is caught off the coast of this country. When you realize that 60 per cent of it is thrown away once it is caught, you begin to realize what a socio-economic problem we have, and that there is a number of things that would be required to be done by this Government to solve that problem. The fact is that you can sell only female
March 8, 1985

capelin because that is what the Japanese want. You have a Japanese shaker in every fish plant. The female herring continue along; the male herring go down a chute into the salt water and are thrown away.
Shame!
Oh, come on!

All right, I congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary and the Minister. We will see down the road just how good he is. He has been making fine statements, but I do not like his cuts. It is unfortunate that I do not have the time to deal with them. This is an incredible problem with which we are dealing. This simple action on the part of the Minister is not good enough because of actions taken by the Government since it came to power. Also it is not good enough because of the appeals which will undoubtedly arise as a result of the inaction and audits of the Department.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member referred to some of the dilemmas in the fishing industry, notably the unemployment which has come about and the problems with the Unemployment Insurance Act. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will listen to this comment as well. It is important to the topic raised.

March 8, 1985
Fisheries Act
In the process of trying to address the question of unemployed fishermen on the West Coast, the Conservative Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) appointed a committee to oversee the disposal of $5 million. That particular committee was appointed by the Minister on the recommendation of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser). As I understand it, they have hired a group of former Conservative organizers from the last federal election. Certainly there are elements of serious concern in terms of patronage and propriety. I would note, for example, an individual by the name of Stan Hagen, a prominent organizer; Jim Lorney, a prominent organizer; and Thor Petersen. They have been named as individuals to oversee this committee. Has the Hon. Member had any experiences of a similar nature in his riding where political patronage has been similar?

Mr. Speaker, I cannot point toward any political patronage which has occurred so far. I notice they changed the board of directors of Fisheries Products International since the Minister of Justice took office. His brother was removed from the chairmanship of the board. I cannot see any influence being exerted there by the Government of Canada as far as appointments are concerned.
I am not too concerned about political patronage, but when we have a Government which professes to do certain things which are perceived to be for the public good, what should be examined by the Chamber and by its committees is their impact on ordinary people. For example, when we decide to try to cut back on unemployment insurance and just do audits, as I mentioned in my speech, we have to realize the ramifications; people who are innocent could end up being found guilty and having to pay back enormous sums of money. We have to look at what happens down the chain. We cannot, as the Government announced, close a $30 million laboratory facility or cancel vessels for research at $18.1 million. The technological laboratory in Vancouver will be closed. It is intended that the technical and scientific staff will be reassigned within the Department. Really that is not an excuse; we have to look at the long term. I notice that the Minister says:
The recently-created task force headed by the Hon. Erik Nielsen intends to consult with the provinces and the private sector to determine which other areas of activities or programs might need restructuring.
The point is that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans really does not deserve the treatment that he is getting from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret). This Minister is trying honestly to do his job. He has been associated with the fisheries for years. Now he is being frowned upon by the fishermen. He is being chastised in practically every home in certain parts of the country, all because of the actions of the Minister of Finance, the President of the Treasury Board and other Cabinet Ministers. I do not really think it is fair to treat the Minister of Fisheries in that manner.

Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of the House, I am wondering if the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate
(Mr. Baker), because of his long-established knowledge of the fishing industry and particularly some of the various federal departments associated with that industry, would share with us his views with regard to other possible conflicts between the Fisheries Act and these amendments. While we are attempting to assist the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser), it is important that we know what those conflicts are so that we can try to resolve or reconcile them to the benefit of the people we are supposed to serve. I would therefore ask the Hon. Member that question.

Mr. Speaker, in the short time available I will deal with definitions. I could go anywhere in the Act. When you look at the Act, you see that the regulations under the Unemployment Insurance Commission describe kelp. Let us get down to the catch, the fish, the natural product or by-product of the ocean. It includes Irish moss, kelp and whales, but does not include fish scales. It includes kelp and Irish moss. That is a definition of fish under the Act. Somebody who walks out into the water and catches a capelin which drifts ashore is not insurable under the definition of fisherman, but somebody can walk out and rake up kelp on the ocean floor or in a river basin and he is a fisherman. That person is a fisherman, but somebody who does it from the shore is not. There have been innumerable cases before the courts.
Fresh catch is defined as a catch that is not cured. There have been cases which arose from that because cod liver is listed as cured fish but shark liver is not. You go back and you judge that somebody should not have received unemployment insurance because the division was wrong.
The definition of "fisherman" is a person engaged in making a catch, but it also includes people doing incidental work related to that catch. In other words, let us look at judges' decisions in the Province of Nova Scotia, where the Hon. Member who asked the question is from. There was the case of Phyllis Karsten and Catherine Stevens v. The Minister of National Revenue. In that judgment, the Chief Justice said that by reason of performing the tasks, these tasks include cutting bait and baiting hooks. The point is that it was not done in the boat. It was done on the shore.
There are these problems within the Act. Women in this case are saying that they bait hooks. So does somebody in the boat. You need do only one thing to cure that problem. You need just put in one line that says you must have been in a boat. You would not then have these appellants having to pay back $10,000 to the federal Government. There are many other cases. I do not have time to go into them because my time has expired.
My original point is this. When a problem arises, MPs from this Chamber have to go to their districts and defend constituents who must repay money to the federal Government. We have been doing that for years. When you look at other judgments that have been made, it could be a massive problem. However, no changes are made to the Act. When the Department of Fisheries has been slighted, changes have been brought before the House of Commons and they have been
March 8, 1985

passed forthwith. That is what the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans should be examining.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mel Gass (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, sometimes when a Member is going full flight, he should be allowed to carry on. I appreciate the comments being made by the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) regarding UIC and the fact that there are problems. I agree almost 100 per cent with the Member when he talks about the problems of UIC and Revenue Canada. I have had the same experience with the previous Government and the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act with regard to the Minister of National Revenue making the final decision. With a new Minister, I hope some changes will be made and some of the problems with UIC will be corrected as they relate to fishermen and the fact that the Minister of National Revenue has the final say after the fact. I know from experience where five years after the fact people have had to pay back money because the Minister of National Revenue said the person was not eligible as a result of some circumstance that happened four or five years previously which the person could not prove.
I am off the point I am supposed to be speaking on, namely Bill C-32, an Act to amend the Fisheries Act.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) made special mention of the roe herring industry in British Columbia. He has pointed out its great importance this year. For those Hon. Members who are not from the Pacific coast and who may not be familiar with the roe herring fishery, it may be difficult to visualize the challenges and rewards that management of this fishery involves.
Certainly in terms of its tempo and its intensity, the roe herring fishery is unique. The prize in this fishery is not the fish but the roe, the eggs. Herring roe is a gourmet item in Japan. It is, so to speak, the caviar of Tokyo. The price Fishermen get for the catch depends on the maturity of the roe. The trick is to catch the herring at precisely the right moment, figuratively speaking, at the eleventh hour and fifty-ninth second before spawning.
The herring season has opened on the West Coast. We had two seasons, one on Wednesday which lasted four hours and ten minutes and one that started at nine o'clock this morning British Columbia time. It will end when the quota is reached in that area.
A large British Columbia fleet takes part in this fishery, 241 seiners and more than 1,300 gillnetters. To succeed in this fishery, timing has to be exquisite. The stakes are so high that many boats take up position on the fishing grounds well in advance of the opening. That is in case the herring show up a little earlier than expected. If they show up late, that means higher costs and dead time. If they show up very late or not at all, it could be a catastrophe. February and March are tense months for herring fishermen in British Columbia.
Fisheries Act
The roe herring fishery starts very early in the year in San Francisco Bay. Then it moves north with the spring to other parts of the coast. The first Canadian roe fisheries off the west coast of Vancouver Island and in Georgia Strait began, as I said, yesterday. The last one before the stocks pass on into Alaskan waters is at the end of March on the north coast around Prince Rupert.
The intensity of this fishery is legendary. There have been years when a roe herring fishery in a given area has been opened for just 15 minutes. The competition in this limited fishery is tremendous. One of the management challenges is to balance the interests and efforts of the two gear types used in this Fishery, gillnetters and seiners. It might be interesting to note that of the two seasons that began this year, one was for seiners and one was for gillnetters. The seiners generally work in deep water. They are powerful harvesting machines. It is not unusual for a seine boat to take 600 tons in one set. The gillnetters work closer to shore with fixed gear and their capacity is much lower: about 1 per cent of the seiners. Part of the problem is to balance the interests and impact of these two different gear types. To do that we have to be able to regulate by gear type and by area.
There is another aspect to the challenge that also demands precise fishery management. Herring stocks have a reputation for instability. In 1965 there was a massive stock collapse that put an end to the fishmeal industry. In the long run, things turned out well. In 1972, when Japan's herring stocks were in decline, the B.C. industry was able to get a foothold in a much more lucrative market. Fishermen had been getting $11 per ton for herring used for fishmeal. In recent years they have been getting as much as $900 per ton for the roe. In fact, the price this year is $812 per ton.
The basic volatility is still there, however. As the Minister pointed out, some of the stocks are depleted. The fishery off the west coast of Vancouver Island has been closed and the fishery in Georgia Strait has been curtailed. This is a prudent and necessary action. We do not know all of the reasons for the ups and downs of the herring. Some scientists think it may be related to the infusion of warm currents known as El Nino. Whatever the cause, we know we have to be doubly careful not to over-fish the stocks.
It comes down to this, Mr. Speaker: we have a resource of immense value. We have an industry built on that resource which in B.C. is second in size only to the salmon industry. We have a complex fishery concentrated in time and location, conducted by competing gear types. We have a resource that requires careful management.
If, as this fishery gets under way, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans' authority to manage the fishery or the validity of the fishing plan developed with the industry is challenged because of a possible deficiency or lack of clarity in the wording of the Act, there may be very serious consequences for Fishermen, for the industry and for the resource. With the salmon industry in difficulty, an efficient roe herring fishery is

March 8, 1985
Fisheries Act
essential. We should make sure that its performance is not hindered by uncertainties in the Act. We can remove that danger by making the revisions proposed. I hope Members will do so without further delay.

Mr. Speaker, I heard the speech made by the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary. While we are dealing with a fisheries Bill, I would like to comment on the tremendous importance not only of the fishing harbours in eastern Canada and the West Coast but as well of the small craft harbours and fishing harbours on the Great Lakes system. In fact, in the Ontario region there are some 450 or even close to 500 fishing harbours and small-craft harbours.
I would like to draw attention to the fact that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the small craft harbours branch have done an excellent job in maintaining these harbours. They not only do a good job of maintaining them under very arduous conditions but they see that they add greatly to the economic activity throughout the Great Lakes Basin.
In my own constituency there are some 45 small craft harbours, representing about 10 per cent of the small craft harbours in the Ontario region. There are a number of harbours used for fishing but a great many are used for small craft activity and provide access to the north channel of Lake Huron which is the best boating and cruising area in North America.
I would call on the Parliamentary Secretary, the Minister who is present in the House and other Hon. Members to add their support to providing financial assistance for the maintenance of small craft harbours and fisheries harbours in the Great Lakes Basin because they are very, very important. I agree completely with what the Hon. Member from Newfoundland who just spoke said, and that is that the Minister is totally dedicated to his Department and to improving and upgrading the harbours. However, he needs the support of the Fisheries Committee and he needs a strong resolution from the Fisheries Committee and from Members of Parliament in order to get adequate funding.
Funding for the Ontario region runs to slightly over $3 million per year. That is simply not adequate to ensure that there is proper maintenance of the small craft harbours. There has been very massive expansion due to the special recovery capital projects in the last two and a half or three years.
There is a main entrance point from Michigan into the north channel of Lake Huron on Meldrum Bay. An iceflow seriously damaged the harbour there and it will require some $70,000 or $80,000 to repair it. I know it is difficult for the Minister to get that kind of funding but I appeal to him to provide that assistance.
For the Minister to have adequate funding not only for the Great Lakes Basin but for the entire country, we as Members must speak up and support him in the Fisheries Committee and in the House to ensure that there is adequate funding to
repair and upgrade all our harbours and particularly those like Meldrum Bay, a main entranceway into the north channel area. As I said, that area is not only a fishing area but a very important boating and sailing area.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the Hon. Member's comments, I can only assure him that we on the Fisheries Committee and we who represent fishing communities on the West Coast, on the Atlantic Coast and on the inland waters of Canada realize that ports, harbours and wharves are essential to fishermen. Fishermen must be able to depart from a safe port and return to a safe port with their catch. I can assure the Hon. Member that that is something about which we are all very concerned even in these times of restraint.
We have to try to be conscious of the dollars that are spent because of the fact that the previous Government wasted so many dollars and set us on a course of no return. We have to cut back everywhere we possibly can, but we must maintain if possible the harbours and wharves that are so essential to the fishermen from one end of the country to the other. In fact, as early as Monday night we are bringing people before the Standing Committee to talk about small craft harbours.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary about a serious matter of which I gave him warning by way of a question, and that is the matter of patronage. I mentioned the individuals concerned and the fact that prominent Conservative organizers now handle jurisdiction over the approximately $5 million that is intended to be spent on projects to aid unemployed fishermen. I would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary if-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That is a point of order. The subject matter brought up by the Hon. Member is not related to the Bill. I am stopping the Hon. Member at this point because it is obviously not related to the Bill before us today. It is neither related to the speech made by the Hon. Member nor to the Bill itself.

Mr. Speaker, I would rise on a point of order and take a moment to point out to you that the previous speaker mentioned serious economic concerns of fishermen. The point I am coming to is that that particular group has been charged with the responsibility of dealing with the economic concerns of Fishermen by using this money, and that the Minister failed to conduct any meaningful consultation with fisheries groups, community groups or any other groups that may be affected. This particular point of order is vitally important because we do not want to see this kind of thing happening. I hope you will recognize my right to ask the Parliamentary Secretary a question, Mr. Speaker. Will the Government continue to appoint political hacks rather than move ahead to widespread consultation? That consultation is not happening.
After I have made my point of order, may I have an opportunity to ask a question of the Parliamentary Secretary on a matter directly related to this issue?
March 8, 1985

speechtext: I will permit the question. However, as I have pointed out, I have reservations concerning its relevance in the large interpretation. I will permit the question but 1 would hope that the Hon. Member will bear that in mind.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might just correct the record by indicating that the individuals who are involved are experienced, knowledgeable and have integrity. The point of the matter is that consultation is a factor which is important. I do not wish to criticize those people in any way, but the way in which the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) went about this appointment was absolutely wrong.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot take responsibility for appointments which are made by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). Neither can I take responsibility for the appointments which are recommended by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser). I have no knowledge of the appointments which have allegedly taken place. However, if members of the Liberal Party and members of the NDP would let this Bill out of the House today, they could put those questions to the Minister in the standing committee next Tuesday.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to direct a question to the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker). However, we ran out of time, so I will bootleg it to the Parliamentary Secretary.
In his speech, the Parliamentary Secretary mentioned that not enough money had been devoted to fisheries research. I presume he was speaking about the last 16 years. As I am a new Member, I wonder if he could tell me if it is indeed a fact that not enough money has been devoted toward research in the fisheries. Second, he wondered whether socio-economic grounds should come into play in the Fisheries Act. Is it not true that the majority of legislation in the House of Commons is based on socio-economic grounds? If so, why should the Fisheries Act be an exception?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize it is an important question and one which would take a long time to answer. Again, I would remind the Hon. Member that the question could be more appropriately put to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. If this Bill could be given second reading today, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans could be before the committee as early as next Tuesday and he would be able to answer those questions. Then we could get on with this Bill, which is very important to the fishing industry of Canada because of the uncertainty which exists due to the two decisions which were rendered by a judge. The intent of this Bill is to remove uncertainty in the minds of Canadians as to whether or not the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has the right to allocate fish stocks to different sectors of gear type and different areas.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: In resuming debate, I will recognize the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly).

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-32, although I regret the haste with which the Government is attempting to push this legislation through the House. The Government says that the legislation must be passed in a hurry because of the herring season. The herring season opened two days ago for seiners on the West Coast and it is open today for gill netters. The rush and fury of the herring season, which the Minister and Parliamentary Secretary described, seems to have infected the Government. It is introducing this Bill in a similar manner of rush and fury, expecting the legislation to pass very quickly. I do not think the Government is going to do that. I think it is in for a long haul, unless it is prepared to give certain assurances to the House. This last minute tabling, and the Government's indicating that we are up against a deadline, is the sort of activity that we used to get from the Liberal Government. It encourages a degree of cynicism and makes parliamentarians look somewhat irresponsible. Our Party does not intend to submit to that kind of blackmail.
Bill C-32 will increase the power of the Department to control the fishery but, at the same time, the Estimates which were tabled a week ago decreased the ability of the Department to manage the fishery in a rational manner.
Incidentally, we do have some good news. I think the Minister has been too modest in some of the things which he has done. He is responsible for a net increase of one-third in the fisheries habitat over the last week. If we looked at the Estimates which were tabled on February 26, we would see that there are 1,500 rivers on the West Coast which are capable of spawning salmon. However, in the Minister's speech a week later he indicated that 2,000 rivers were capable of doing that. The increase of 500 rivers within a week is the first sign of any real activity we have had from the Minister since his appointment.
I would like to ask a question in a rhetorical way, and maybe the Conservatives would like to answer it in a rhetorical way. If Romeo LeBlanc or Pierre De Bane had brought in this legislation in the previous Government, would members of the Conservative Party have supported it? I suspect the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) would have been among the first, after the New Democrats, to oppose it.
Bill C-32 is as arbitrary and high-handed as the salmon treaty which was recently concluded with the United States. As my colleague has pointed out, that treaty was rushed through Cabinet in half an hour. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had not read it, but he knew that he wanted the treaty so he would be able to sign it with President Reagan on St. Patrick's Day in Quebec City. That illustrates the arbitrary nature of what is happening.
We could look at what that treaty has done in relation to the sports fishery. There are 300,000 to 400,000 sports fishermen in British Columbia. The treaty indicates that within the Strait

March 8, 1985
Fisheries Act
of Georgia there will be an annual catch of 275,000 Chinook. That catch has to be shared between the sports fishery and the trollers. Sports fishermen were previously entitled to four Chinook a day, or a total of 30 Chinook per season. When the Department was first studying the treaty, it considered a limit of one Chinook per day, or a total of five per season. However, under pressure from the sports fishing industry, the number was increased to two Chinook per day, or a total of 20 per season. That seems to be a reasonable compromise.
We recognize the importance of the sports fishing industry, but we must recognize that that compromise is not without some very serious problems. There is still an upper limit of 275,000 Chinook which must be shared between gulf trollers and sports fishermen. Not all 400,000 sports fishermen are salt-water fishermen, and not all of them fish in the Strait of Georgia, but that is where the bulk of the fishing takes place. The official designation for the Strait of Georgia includes everything from Sherringham Point on the west coast of Vancouver Island, to Chatham Point, which is located north of the Campbell River. If there were only 150,000 sports fishermen in that area, the total allocation would not give them one day's catch of two Chinook each. That does not leave anything for the gulf trollers. Gulf trollers generally have small boats and cannot fish on the dangerous west coast of Vancouver Island, so they require a share of the Chinook in the Strait of Georgia.
Because of the mild climate on the coast, sports fishing has year-round potential, not only as recreation but also as an industry. Once the 275,000 Chinook limit is reached, the industry will be closed down. That limit includes both natural and enhanced stock. In a letter to me, the Minister said that the limit could be raised "if there is an improvement in the strength of runs of natural Chinook stocks". But how about enhanced stocks? If there is a great improvement in enhanced stock over the next few years, the 275,000 limit will remain. If there are more fish, it will take much less time for the sports fishermen and the trollers to reach the total allocation. When total allocation is reached, the sports fishery will be closed. That will mean financial ruin for marina operators and others who depend upon it.
The treaty has now been approved by the United States Congress and is ready for signature on March 17. It is worth nothing, Mr. Speaker, that the United States administration has not put any dollars on the table to make sure that it is able to live up to its part of the bargain. This fact was brought out by Mr. Don Bonker, a Washington State Democrat, who is concerned that the United States might fall short of its obligation with regard to the salmon fishing treaty.
The arbitrary means by which the Conservative Government approved the treaty is fully consistent with the arbitrary nature of this Bill. There was no consultation. We recognize the necessity of management and of allocation. We recognize that there is great pressure on a limited resource. But we raise the question of how that management should take place. This
is an important question, Mr. Speaker. On February 3 of last year, when the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans was in opposition, he raised that question when he moved a motion of non-confidence in the Liberal Government. Throughout his speech on February 3 of last year, he stressed the need for industry involvement and management. He said, and I quote from page 1055 of Hansard, February 3, 1984:
The third imperative is industry participation in fisheries management. This must be something much more than mere consultation.
The present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans went on to say:
What we have in mind is an industry management board appointed by the respective user groups to determine policy and to report directly to the Minister. Policy recommendations, with the rationale for them, should be made public. This is the only way the difficult decisions, impinging on one group or another as they will under current circumstances, can ever be made to work. The immediate advantage to this is that those who know the most about the industry and the impact of decisions on the industry will be formulating the policy. The insistence that their deliberations be made public will guarantee accountability.
Later in his speech he said:
-we would recommended that the Government establish an industry management board with representation from all segments of the industry, including the sports fisherman ... If we are going to do that, as I have urged, that industrial management board must have some clout. It must be respected. The policy options that it works out must be treated seriously by the Government.
The Minister also called for buy-back and building habitat. He talked about the importance of the salmonid enhancement program. He said that second stage salmonid enhancement program funding should be brought forward immediately for this purpose. There is no reference in the speech of the Minister last year to increasing the berthage fees for vessels at the docks of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. There is no reference to privatizing the fishing vessel insurance plan. These are two things about which we now hear.
There is nothing in this Bill, Mr. Speaker, and nothing that the Minister has done since taking office last fall, that has addressed the urgent problems which he outlined last February. Where is the commitment to open Government about which we heard so much last spring and during the election campaign? Where is the commitment to real participation in management of the fisheries which the Minister talked about when he was in opposition? Where are the decisions which are going to be made by different user groups? Where is the buy-back to reduce the excess fishing capacity in the industry? Where is the increased habitat protection? Where is the salmonid enhancement program?
It is interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, that shortly after the Minister was appointed he was interviewed by the United Fishermen Allied Workers Union and he said that he was committed to a buy-back program as soon as possible, and to increasing funding for salmonid enhancement. He said that if the buy-back program could not get legislative approval in short order, he would proceed without it. One of his first announcements after taking over his new post was to call for an industrial board to advise the Minister on Fisheries matters. However, details of the board structure have not yet been worked out. That was back in September, Mr. Speaker, and the board's structure has still not been worked out. We find
March 8, 1985

that this Minister, who had and still has a good reputation as a progressive within his own Party, is going right along with the cut-back mentality of his Government. I believe that some of the progressives within the Cabinet are going to have to sit down together at some point and ask their consciences how long they can continue to go along with the general direction of this Government, which runs completely counter to the sort of things they in their hearts believe in. Although the Minister is from the Pacific coast, 4.4 per cent was cut from the budget of the fisheries on the Pacific coast as compared to 1.5 per cent cuts to the fisheries of the Atlantic coast. We do not expect patronage just because the Minister is from the Pacific coast but we would like to see at least some equity.
On the Pacific coast the fishery research has been cut almost 30 per cent, from $17.5 million to $12.5 million. That is a loss of 31 person years. Fisheries management will have 18 fewer people to do the kinds of jobs which are needed if the fishery is going to be properly looked after. At the very time that the Bill is giving the Department more responsibilty to regulate the fishery, the Minister is reducing its capability to do so in an informed and intelligent manner. The salmonid enhancement program remains stuck in second gear of the transition phase.
Without any regulations which require input from user groups, the Department will be given the right to regulate the industry in the most minute ways and in a manner which can spell economic life or death for the people who are involved in the fishery. The Minister made a commitment that there was going to be involvement of user groups, but now we see that there is an arbitrary power being given to the Department and its employees. The Minister asked for this power so that he could treat all segments of the industry in a fair manner. However, I am sure that the Minister would not have wanted to give this kind of power to his predecessor. I am sure that he would not want to give this power to any successor from another Party because it places too much power by far in the hands of the Minister and his Department without any kind of checks or balances.
I would like to say a few words about the rights of the aboriginal people. There is nothing in this Act which speaks to their needs or reassures them with respect to their aboriginal rights. Hon. Members of this House should know-they have been told a number of times in the last couple of weeks-that the reserves in British Columbia were very small when created because government officials recognized that Indian people in British Columbia depended for their livelihood upon the ocean and rivers and upon the regular runs of salmon and other fish. For that reason the reserves, when created, were very small. They have very little economic viability apart from their access to the fishery, yet there is nothing in this Bill which recognizes their right. Several British Columbia aboriginal tribes look out to the ocean and stake some of their claims there, but this Bill does not recognize or deal with that.
We have concern about Clause 2 of the Bill which alters the purposes of the Fisheries Act. Clause 2.1(d) reads:
Fisheries Act
To provide, in co-operation with the provinces, for the proper management, allocation and control of the inland fisheries of Canada.
This opens the way for provincial involvment and control of inland fisheries, which can have a very negative impact upon some of the rights of the Indian people who live upstream. The sweeping nature of this clause leads us to request that the Minister either delete it or else bring in some kind of acceptable amendment.
I understand that there is also some question about the congruence of the English and French version of this Bill. I am neither a lawyer nor an expert in the French language so I do not intend to go into any detail on that. I simply want to flag it. I hope that the appropriate people will study that and ensure that the English and French versions are brought into line with each other.
In conclusion, before we give the Minister the power for which he has asked in this Act, we want to have some reassurances from him that there will be regulations ensuring a proper allocation to the native people, some guarantee of their right to fish. We want assurances that there will be commitments to the different communities on the coast so that allocations will not discriminate against one community in favour of another to ensure that all parts of the coast are treated fairly. We want assurances that there will be guidelines tabled to enable us to understand how allocations will take place. We want assurances that there will be some mechanism for co-management as the Minister promised. I urge the Minister to be forthcoming in these respects as soon as possible so that, as he requests, this Bill can get out of the House and into committee where it can be properly addressed.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) on a question or comment.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested to learn, from the remarks of the previous speaker in his excellent presentation, that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mul-roney) had not even read the treaty when he urged that it be signed and dealt with very quickly. I recall the time when we discovered that the Cabinet had passed this very complex, important document in 30 minutes, that the Prime Minister accused the NDP of trying to force the country backward. I am now shocked to learn that the Prime Minister had not even read the document. The second thing that amazes me is that they spent most of the time in that Cabinet meeting discussing where they would get the $8 million to pay for the administration.
Would the previous speaker give the House an indication of whether the Prime Minister has read the document to this date? I know it is on record that he wanted that document very badly, as it appears in the news release. Yet, until the point in time when the Cabinet approved it, he had not even read the document. Does the Hon. Member know whether he has read it to this day?

March 8, 1985
Fisheries Act

Mr. Speaker, I cannot say whether the Prime Minister has read the document. However, I would like to point out that while there has been some discussion as to whether the $8 million would be forthcoming, there has been no indication in the United States that the money they need to implement the treaty will be forthcoming.
My hon. friend has just pointed out that the increase in moorage will match exactly the $8 million needed to administer the treaty. Therefore, fishermen, who are facing a very difficult economic time right now, are being charged extra moorage costs which they cannot avoid in order to pay for the administration of this treaty, which, as my friend has pointed out at different times, seriously impinges upon the sovereignty of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin my remarks on Bill C-32 with a very unusual statement coming from this side of the House. I would like to congratulate the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister (Mr. Gass). I would like to wish them well in carrying out their responsibilities of administering a fisheries program for all of Canada. I say that very sincerely because I want the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans for Canada to be successful. It is important to my region of the country that the fisheries and the fisheries programs instituted by the national Government be successful. I do not think that any Member of Parliament, regardless of his or her political affiliation, would want to see the Minister or his very able Parliamentary Secretary not be successful. We want the complete opposite. I hope he will be successful. I will indicate some areas, Mr. Speaker, in which Members in this Chamber, including Members of his own Party, can be beneficial and very helpful to the Minister and the Department in assisting them in carrying out their mandate.
In reading through this short Bill I was interested to read its purposes. One of the purposes stated in the Bill is worth bringing to the attention of all Members. It is a far-reaching purpose acknowledged solely because the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans understands the complexities of this particular Department and the linkages which that Department has with the economies of the West and East Coasts. It is stated in Clause 2.1(c):
The purposes of this Act are
(c) to ensure a continuing supply of fish and to maintain and develop the
economic and social benefits from the use of fish to fishermen and others
employed in the Canadian seacoast fishing industry.
That is a very far-reaching purpose in a federal statute. The Minister has said that the reason for these amendments is that:
The Fisheries Act itself does not clearly provide the federal Government with the powers for full fisheries management. Bill C-32 will confirm the ability of the federal Government to fulfil such a full range of modern day responsibilities.
He went on to say that:
-the amendments to Bill C-32 are needed to confirm and to clarify our authority under the Fisheries Act to make decisions reconciling all these competing interests.
And I emphasize the word "competing", Mr. Speaker. The Minister went on to say that:
Fisheries management involves not just resource goals but also social and economic goals.
Very clearly, Mr. Speaker, as stated in the clause on the purposes of the Act and by the Minister responsible for the Act, social and economic goals are part and parcel of a fisheries policy for Canada. I want to flag that because it is important. When one looks at the other agencies and Departments of the national Government, there seems to be a void. They are not, in my opinion-and I stand to be corrected- fulfilling the substantive portions of the enactment and of the Minister's statement.
I will give you an example. What about the provisions of unemployment insurance? My colleague, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twiilingate (Mr. Baker), made mention of some of the changes and other things which are tied to the Unemployment Insurance Act and how that affects fishermen. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), sent out signals across the country that he wants to haul back on the Unemployment Insurance Commission payments. For a fisherman living on UIC, SI50 a week is not much. These signals sent out by the Minister of Finance are different from those sent out by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. It is one thing to tell the middle class of Canada, who make $25,000 or $30,000 a year, that there are going to be changes. They can provide for their food and lodging. However, it is a different matter for the Minister of Finance to tell those receiving $150 a week in unemployment insurance that he is going to shorten their period of insurable earnings and they will get less money. Do you know what that means to someone who must buy the milk and pay for the rent and heat? It is a devastating feeling to sit in your home, available and ready to work but unable to find work, and to have the Minister of Finance say on the floor of the House of Commons that the Government is considering and will ask questions about how it can save more money on unemployment insurance. I say to the Minister in all sincerity that that is certainly not in the best interest of the recipient of UIC, whether it is a fisherman or someone else. It is a devastating feeling. The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) are sending out many different signals throughout the country which have a real effect on the fishermen on the East Coast and the West Coast.
Another agency that has a competing interest working against fishermen rather than for their benefit is the Department of National Revenue. Perhaps it is acceptable for Members of Parliament, some of whom may be legal scholars, to talk about audits conceptually. However, for those who make a small amount of money, often below the poverty level, it is tantamount to harassment to have some bureaucrat, at the instruction of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty) or in co-operation with the Minister of Employment and Immigration, say that the Department will do a lengthy and detailed audit of their earnings over a period of time. This may
March 8, 1985

be acceptable conceptually, but the reality is that those individuals are facing harassment. There can be nothing more distasteful or repugnant than to have a national Government zeroing in on the unemployed-fishermen or anyone else. We can agree that abuses must be corrected, but National Revenue, in its attitude to fishermen in auditing their claims, has gone too far. I hope the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, the Minister of National Revenue and their colleagues will consider that issue.
The Minister talks about social and economic concerns. The Department of Regional Industrial Expansion is a substantive and very important body in terms of the lifeblood of Atlantic Canadians. We are worried in Atlantic Canada that the Minister responsible for that Department is not acting in co-operation with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Some weeks ago, 1 brought to the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that a fire destroyed a fish plant in my constituency. Of course, there were musings from the Minister of Employment and Immigration that help would be forthcoming to rebuild that plant, but nothing has taken place except for a few studies.
My point is that the intent of this legislation cannot be left to one Minister of the Crown to carry out. There must be a collective will to do so, and I urge Members of Parliament, particularly government Members, to impress upon their colleagues and respective Ministers to take cognizance of the purpose of the Act.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has pledged his support for the fishermen and their interests. However, notwithstanding his comments about unemployment insurance, the Minister of Finance has made substantial cut-backs with regard to the Deparment of Fisheries and Oceans. I suggest that a Government that strongly supports a resource industry would not implement cut-backs as the present Government has done. For example, with respect to capital expenditures alone, there has been a deferral of phase 3 of the construction of the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Centre in Saint John's. This is a substantial cut, although it may seem insignificant to those who are not familiar with the fishing industry. I urge government Members not to allow the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister to hang the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans out on a limb, because that is what they are doing. They are not permitting the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to have the tools to do his job, as evidenced by the deferral of the construction of the new fisheries lab in West Vancouver and the deferral of the construction of a new district fisheries building in New Brunswick.
It is time for Government back-benchers to speak up, because I firmly believe that the Government cannot state a certain intent in a federal statute and then do the exact opposite. Another example is the Scotia-Fundy Fisheries Centre which will be deferred for four years. That is a facility which would greatly contribute to the enhancement of opportunities for fishermen and people in the industry. There are many more cuts.
Fisheries Act
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) wants to cut the deficit. Rather than go to Bay Street to cut the deficit, he singles out the fishermen. He will not build more wharves or give them the much needed infrastructure when the livelihood of the fishermen depends on a good facility. However, neither the Minister of Finance nor other Ministers of the Government have a vision of this country. He does not share, as we in this party and, I am sure, certain Members on that side of the House, the view that the fishing industry of Canada is important to the Canadian economy and absolutely vital to the regions of this country. The Minister of Finance has taken actions which are completely opposite to what the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has stated publicly, and they are also opposite to what is stated in the Act.
Again I say to government Members that if they are going to vote in favour of this legislation and its objectives, I suggest that they advise the Minister of Finance to live up to those objectives.
Finally, in the last number of years we have seen a proliferation of regulations both at the provincial and the federal levels. There are approximately 17 statutes which are administered by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. It is one thing to enact a piece of legislation, but we must remember those whom we are attempting to serve. What is this legislation for? It is to have regulation after regulation after regulation made by the vehicle of Order in Council, much of which is not known by many individuals. Yes, we have the argument time and time again that a regulation is gazetted and that it goes out to the regions, and if anyone wants it they can call up and get it. The fact is that there are a lot of confused individuals who, through no fault of their own, are not aware of the regulations nor of their effects and how they operate. I will quote one individual talking about regulations, a professor of law at Dalhousie University, who said that great administrative discretion allows federal officials to alter fishing regulations and policy almost overnight. A lack of a legislative mandated consultation process allows officials to chart a fishery management policy virtually on the basis of plans of their own design subject only to the advice of their own choosing.
I think that tells it all, Mr. Speaker. We do not want a proliferation of regulation for the sake of regulation. If there has to be regulation, it ought to be meaningful. Before you arrive at that level of legislation-because that is what it is, let us make no mistake about that-there ought to be a meaningful consultation process. It does not have to be a process which is long and cumbersome, but there has to be a process, both to communicate the intended result about what the regulation is supposed to achieve and also for the general knowledge of the active players in the fishing industry. It is important for them to know first hand both the content of what regulations may be and the effects of that legislation.
I want to conclude because I have a gentlemen's agreement with my colleague, who no doubt will get up and support

everything I have said. I want to have the record show that I agreed to speak until a quarter to four-
