Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the Hon. Member's assertion that the Minister is trying to do a good job. That fits with my recollection of the Minister speaking on this matter in the House last year in his role as Fisheries and Oceans critic, but whether he was the critic or not, he was certainly active on this subject. I remember that at that time the Minister was very interested in having the greatest amount of consultation possible with the fishermen before the legislation was passed. Could the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) comment on whether there has been the kind of consultation to his knowledge, because he knows a great deal more about this than I do, that would enable this legislation to be more practicable, or would he suggest that that consultation might still be obtained?

Briefly, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe there has been any meaningful consultation. I believe there has been consultation by the Minister in terms of his travels across the country in meeting with the various provincial Ministers of fisheries and the various interested groups. In terms of actually debating and having briefs which will be submitted on various points, hopefully we will be able to get some of that information through the process of committee. I would say in cursory fashion that if there had been consultations, then why were there such devastating cut-backs in the November 8 economic statement to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans? I do not find too many fishermen writing to me saying that they agree with these cut-backs, both in terms of the capital and the operating expenditures of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. There is not a fishermen that I know of in Atlantic Canada who will write and say, "Yes, we want to have our special recovery program terminated", whether it is to build a wharf or something else. There was no consultation.
The answer to the Hon. Member's question is that I do not believe there was meaningful consultation. Hopefully, because
of the attitude of the Minister there will be much more meaningful consultation in the future.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg).

Mr. Speaker, it is customary for a Member of Parliament during his maiden speech to sign the praises of his or her particular riding. Far be it from me to break this tradition.
Nanaimo-Alberni has been called Canada's paradise, with its temperate climate and inherent scenic beauty from Nanaimo on the east coast of Vancouver Island to the rain forest of the Pacific Rim National Park on the west coast. It is also a very busy place, Mr. Speaker. It is the scene of the world famous Nanaimo to Vancouver bathtub race. It is said that Nanaimo has the cleanest politicians around. The salmon capital of the world is located in Port Alberni. Parksville-Qualicum is the site of the world croquet championship. It is also the former riding of one of the world's great statesmen, Mr. Tommy Douglas.
There is a dark side to the beauty of Nanaimo-Alberni, and it is one of the main reasons I would like to speak today on Bill C-32.
In an area dependent on the resources sector, the logging of trees and the harvesting of fish, unemployment is as high as 30 per cent in Nanaimo-Alberni. That, Mr. Speaker, is unacceptable. The fishermen in my riding are counting on our new Government to manage the resource properly and to improve the economic prospects of the West Coast fishermen, or fisherpersons as one Hon. Member has stated. Unfortunately, many of our fishing methods have been around for the last one hundred years. They are very much out of date and changes have to come. This Bill represents a modest change.
I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in the debate on second reading of Bill C-32, an Act to amend the Fisheries Act. We on this side of the House had hoped we could still get speedy consideration at all stages. This Bill is housekeeping legislation. I am quoting the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey). It is a straightforward, unambiguous Bill intended, first, to confirm the Minister's powers to manage the fisheries in all its dimensions and, second, to refine the on-site management powers assigned under the Act to fisheries managers.
I was rather disturbed by some of the objections raised by members of the two opposition Parties in Wednesday's debate. I think they are labouring under some misapprehensions about the implications of the Bill-misapprehensions which I hope to dispel this afternoon. I am equally concerned when they say they cannot pass this urgently needed legislation until the whole gamut of issues affecting the fisheries on both coasts has been aired.
Let us establish at the outset what this Bill is about. Essentially, it has two thrusts. First, it removes any statutory ambiguity concerning the Minister's powers under the Act to undertake the full management of the fishery. It does this by
March 8, 1985

spelling out clearly the purposes of the Act and by up-dating the definitions of fish and fishery in the Act to make them more comprehensive. It confirms what people who know the fishery have always known, that is, that true management of our fisheries means management for social and economic benefit and not for conservation alone.
Second, the Bill refines the on-site management powers available to local fishery managers to allow them, among other things, to open or close portions of a management area where now they must open or close entire areas.
Let us be clear. There are no vast new powers conferred by this Bill. To quote again the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, this Bill "simply enshrines in law what the Department felt it could do all along".
It sounds like an excellent Bill.

It is. Many of us were surprised that these powers were disputed in a court of law, but since they have been disputed, that shadow of doubt must be lifted. These amendments do just that.
None of the three Parties in the House has questioned the need for these powers. The Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) in a speech in this Chamber on Wednesday indicated, in terms of the denial of these powers to the Minister, the following:
-to me spells complete chaos in the fisheries management regime, not just on the West Coast but on the East Coast as well . . . We must amend this legislation to provide an orderly management regime in the fishing industry.
That makes sense.

It does. The second major provision concerning on site management powers for fishery managers similarly refines existing delegated powers rather than conferring new ones. As I just remarked, currently fishery managers must make judgments about opening or closing entire management areas to fishing. If a particular endangered stock is found in one small corner of a given area, the entire area may have to be closed and fishermen denied access to fish stocks throughout that area, just to conserve the endangered stock.
Opening and closing sub-areas is possible under the current Act, but the decision cannot be taken on site. It requires a lengthy process of enactment by Order in Council a slow and cumbersome process which inhibits effective fisheries management. The process can take weeks, and we need decisions in hours or even minutes. The provisions of the Bill simply ensure that a fishery manager can act right there on the site, right where a highly changeable situation is unfolding, a situation much like the one the Parliamentary Secretary talked about earlier today in the herring season.
The final point I should like to make about the over-all package is its urgency. The West Coast roe herring fishery has begun. Confirmation of the Minister's management powers is required to ensure the smooth progress of that brief, very lucrative and very competitive fishery.
Fisheries Act
Members of the NDP have said that these powers are not needed for the herring fishery because the major groups have agreed to be bound by the management plan worked out in advance. The Department can take some credit for this, because the Minister and his officials devoted time and energy to developing a workable fishing plan in consultation with the industry. We hope the fishery will proceed without disruption, but it could take just one unhappy fisherman to disrupt that densely packed race for a precious harvest. NDP Members acknowledge that the Minister must have these powers to do his job. Where we part company with them is when they say they will not allow this House to confirm those powers-the framework for fisheries management-until they have a complete accounting of how he plans to allocate among gear types between commercial, sports fishing and native fishermen, of how he plans to address native constitutional and economic issues, and so on. They want to know every detail of how the Minister plans to discharge every facet of his responsibilities now and forever.
They have demanded details on the proposals for a voluntary vessel buy-back, on the next phase of salmonid enhancement, on the settlement of native land claims, on small craft harbours, and on habitat management. If we get into that, we will be discussing this Bill for many days to come. I can tell them that the answers are not available because we are still working them out co-operatively and in close consultation with all affected groups, in line with our commitment to open government.
The opposition Parties claim that we have not adequately considered the people and Parliament on all these issues. That is incorrect. Let me deal with these points in turn. Fisheries management is a consultative process. In the end, Government has to take tough decisions. That is what we are elected to do. Those decisions are tough. They affect the lives and livelihood of literally tens of thousands of individuals in hundreds of communities. They require the reconciliation of closely competing interests of diverse groups, all vying for the same limited resource. But because the issues are so tough and their impact so deep, they have to be resolved collaboratively. On the East Coast, there is an elaborate bottom-up consultative process involving the industry and the provinces. This year the federal groundfish management plan developed by the industry was approved enthusiastically and in a timely fashion by all Atlantic Ministers. Moreover, since taking office, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) has consulted the industry exhaustively on a range of long-term issues.
The Minister has met with the Ministerial Advisory Committee, commonly known as MAC, a body which brings together gillnetters, seiners, trollers, natives, sports fishermen, unions and processors. He has also met groups individually- the Native Brotherhood, the Prince Rupert Fishermen's Cooperative Association, several native bands, the Sports Fishery Advisory Board, and so on. He has met several times with the Fisheries Ministers of the Atlantic provinces and with numerous provincial fishermen's organizations. There is no alternative to putting time and effort into these consultations. This

March 8, 1985
Fisheries Act
commitment to open decision-making will be preserved and strengthened.
The Opposition alleges that the new Fisheries and Oceans Minister has not sufficiently consulted Parliament. That charge is unfair. NDP members of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry had numerous opportunities to bring the Minister before the committee, but they have never availed themselves of those opportunities. The committee had before it the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation amendments, the Saltfish Act amendments and the departmental Supplementary Estimates, but they have never invited the Minister to appear on one of those items.
I urge my colleagues-let us put the essential statutory framework in place. If the Opposition has concerns about the specific provisions of this Bill, let them be put on the record of the House. Let us get down to the business of the Bill, let us leave the rhetoric aside.
I see that I am almost out of time. I should like to point out quickly, as I said earlier, that fishermen on the West Coast have been fishing that way for over a hundred years now. Not everyone likes change, least of all radical change. The fishermen's whole economy is based upon how things are now, so radical change could disrupt many of them. Thus we must be very careful in the measures we initiate in the House and how those measures are initiated.
I have been listening to the comments of my hon. colleagues in the Opposition over the past two days. I know they have a great deal of faith and respect for our new Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. It is not too presumptuous to say that the future of an industry in trouble rests in the hands of the Hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. It has suffered from neglect for too long now. Through this Bill, we are simply asking for the tools to get the job done.
In view of the fact that it is five minutes to the hour, I wonder whether we could simply get the job done and pass this Bill into committee.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I join with other Hon. Members in the House in congratulating the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg) on his maiden speech in the House. Most of us have had that experience. I know he lives in an area which is dependent upon fishing. Would he be in a position to elaborate on a number of issues which he touched upon?
On the Gulf of Georgia there is a serious allocation problem which has been exacerbated by the fact that the Government signed a treaty limiting the total number of Chinook which can be taken. However, it appears that there is a conflict between the gulf trollers and the sports fishing group in the gulf. There appears to be the question of a very serious threat of removing the gulf troller fleet from the gulf entirely. Would the Hon. Member be prepared to go on record as stating that he personally supports the continued existence of a commercial fishery in the Gulf of Georgia?

Mr. Speaker, obviously I am a relatively new Member of the House, but the Hon. Member who has just spoken and several of his colleagues who have been in opposition for years know that the West Coast fishing industry has been in trouble for decades. Very little has been done. We are simply asking for the tools to get the job done. The Pacific salmon treaty was one of the first measures which we could enact to give us the framework so that fishermen could plan for the future. This Bill is another measure or action to enable the Minister to get the job done. We fully support what he is doing in that matter.
As I said earlier, we are running out of time on this. The Minister is prepared to appear before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry next week to answer those kinds of questions. I simply ask my colleagues and the Hon. Member's colleagues to pass this Bill at second reading today.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Hon. Member. He certainly indicated his support for the salmon treaty. Does he support the process by which that treaty came into force in Canada, the fact that Members of Parliament were not allowed to deal with the issue in the House, unlike the American Senate where representatives of the people had a chance to make a judgment on it? Does he in fact support a process wherein Cabinet approves a matter and denies the opportunity for elected representatives to consider it?

Mr. Speaker, I would be pleased to tell the Hon. Member what kind of process I support. I support any process which actually results in action after 18 years of dithering on the salmon treaty. We actually brought action into the House and on that treaty. This Government stands for action, whether it is on this Bill or on the treaty. We stand for action on this Bill today. Again I ask the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River to assist us in passing this Bill into committee.

Mr. Speaker, I had an opportunity in the lobby to see the Hon. Member making his speech, and I congratulate him on it. I thought it was well crafted. I know of his obvious intergrity and sincere interest in fisheries matters. However, I want to say to the Hon. Member that we cannot stand-

speechtext: Is there unanimous consent for the House to proceed to Item No. 59?
Agreed.

That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of introducing a motion to amend the Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982, in order to provide for a major reform of the Senate, so as to ensure that this House is able to fulfil the mandate it was elected to implement without undue interference.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion is vital because, as it is now constituted, the Senate has no place in a democracy. To be a valid democratic legislature, the Senate needs a mandate from the people, and it has no such mandate. The Hon. Stanley Knowles told this House in 1965, and I quote:
We ought to ask ourselves whether there is any place in our parliamentary institution for a group of people who are not responsible to the electors.
In defence of the Senate, there are those who point to the quality of its Members. Of course, Canada is not a meritocracy governed by an elite. It is a democracy whose laws are passed by men and women who have one source for their authority. The Members of this House have a right to determine the direction of Canada. Regardless of our individual talents or lack of them, regardless of our Party strength or lack of it, each of us has the same legislative authority. We have been chosen by the people. We have been given an authority no Senator can ever claim.
Defenders of the Senate have tried to make it acceptable by defining it as a kind of legislative refinery, designed to improve
The Senate
legislation that emanates from the one democratically authorized house, namely the House of Commons.
Bagehot, the 19th century authority on Parliament advocated an Upper House as "a revising and leisurely legislature". In this country, John A. Macdonald wanted it available to check what he called "hasty or ill-considered legislation", to be the so-called "chamber of sober second thought". Let us appreciate, in fairness, that often the Senate has been that in terms of amending and improving legislation, but when we try to defend the Senate as the bulwark of defence for the regions, for the minorities, for the oppressed, we do not have that kind of impressive history to cite.
Let apologists for the Senate admit that it has not been the bulwark for justice they claim. They say the Senate is needed to protect regional interest, but where was the Senate when the national energy policy eviscerated the economy of western Canada? They say the Senate is needed to protect the people's freedoms, but where was the Senate when the War Measures Act was used in 1971 to override civil liberties? They say the Senate is needed to protect minorities, but where was the Senate when Canadians of Japanese origin suffered injustice at the hands of their own Government? The fact is that the Senate has been effective mostly when it has defended privileges, like the privileges of the chartered banks and of the Liberal Party.
Its Liberal majority in the Senate, the only Liberal majority left in the western world, and that solely because it is appointed, has just given us another example of its passion for privilege. Its delay of the borrowing Bill was not a necessary defence of the taxpayers. If that had been necessary, why would the Official Opposition in this House ever have supported passage of the Bill? Yet, it did give support for its passage. I wish to quote from a letter sent by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to the Leader of Opposition (Mr. Turner):
This Bill was not forced through the House by the use of our majority. It passed following an all-Party agreement that had passed the scrutiny and approval of your Caucus.
I cite correspondence from the Government House Leader to his counterpart:
This Order was the result of an agreement made in good faith on behalf of the three parties represented.
The action of the Senate violates the unanimous decision of the House of Commons. The decision was made after full consultation with yourself and your Party's finance critic, Aideen Nicholson, MP, on behalf of the Liberal Caucus.
There was, therefore, no need for the Senate to resurrect its long-neglected power of resisting and vetoing so that it could protect the people of Canada against the tyranny of a majority in this House. The Senate's objective was clear to see for anyone with memories of the Coyne affair. It was to begin a Fabian-like guerrilla war on this elected House and this elected Government, this in spite-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I remind the Hon. Member, and I say this for the benefit of all Members who will intervene in this debate, that the Senate, as the House of Commons, is part of the legislative body of Canada. Therefore, as other Speakers in this Chair have done from time to time, I

March 8, 1985
The Senate
remind distinguished Members of this House that they must be treated with respect. I would carefully remind all Members at this point to act accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, I just point out that I have the utmost respect for Fabius in the ancient world. In likening the Senate majority to Fabius, I was not showing disrespect, but simply pointing out a historical parallel between his ancient style of warfare and what is now being initiated in this Parliament. The action of the Senate-and in no way does this reflect on any individual Member-occurred in spite of the Leader of the Opposition saying to this House words that were permitted by the Speaker in the Chair at that time "I recognize the primacy of the elected House of Commons over the Senate."
This motion was introduced in the hope that it can be passed and that it will not be talked out, for the time for Senate reform is overdue. No one should acknowledge this more than members of the Official Opposition. Senate refrom was a plank in the Liberal platform at the 1919 convention. It was advocated by the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King in the elections of 1925 and 1926. In 1925, King said that reform of the Senate was a necessary bulwark for the preservation of democracy in this country.
I come closer to the present. In 1961, the current Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons, writing an article entitled The Senate-A Political Conundrum, said:
The Senate, in terms of current facts, no longer plays a useful part in the Government of Canada. Its historical purposes have been lost. It no longer operates (albeit through forces beyond the control of its own Members) as a restraining influence on legislation. Its initial historical function, that of representing and protecting the rights and interests of the provinces, were never discharged; and it is scarcely equipped with the necessary mandate for that role today. Consequently, the argument for its abolition is difficult to resist.
The Leader of the Opposition wrote that in 1961. Let him act on it now.
Hear, hear!

His Party has endorsed Senate reform since 1919. Let it use its opportunity now.
Some of us may think that there is little or no hope of action replacing discussion. We count on the support of the Opposition in this Parliament. As the late Right Hon. John Diefen-baker said, Senate reform has been a continuing subject of conversation throughout the years, "something like the weather".
The time for major reform is here as never before. This House has to face the possibility of a Senate using its veto power over legislation. An article in The Toronto Star of February 3, 1985, reads as follows:
Liberal Senator Royce Frith, Deputy Leader of the Opposition in the Senate, says his Party "will not ignore the fact we have a majority ..if legislation is important enough to warrant defeating a Bill.
He is reported to have said that examples of such Bills could be Investment Canada and the reinstatement of capital punishment. That some Members of this House are equally opposed to those measures does not justify an unelected Chamber thwarting the will of this elected House. Certainly, Liberal Members of Parliament should not want it to happen because their Leader has already affirmed the primacy of the elected House of Commons over the Senate. If that primacy is to be taken seriously, the Senate must be reformed. Its potential for vetoing this House must be checked.
We all know the argument for defence which goes that the Senate has not exercised its veto for so many years that only parliamentary historians know when the last time was. Surely that was in part because since 1935, the Liberal majority in the Senate had a Liberal Government to follow in the Commons for 43 of those 50 years. Now there is a Progressive Conservative Government, and since the Thirty-third Parliament opened, this House has heard rumbling sounds rising from the usually dormant Senate. To quote a Member of the other place, Senator Hartland Molson, an independent Senator, has observed:
It's perfectly obvious that what is happening is purely political.
Hubert Bauch in the Montreal Gazette of February 20 reports Senator Molson as saying that with the appointment of so many Trudeau loyalists to the Senate during past years, the Liberals have extended the heated partisanship of the Commons to the Senate.
Now is the time for reforms that can change that situation. One possible change is the proposal that the Senate be elected. This proposal was supported by the Joint Committee on Reform of the Senate in the previous Parliament. According to Senator Michael Pitfield, the Senate cannot perform its function of representing the regions because it is not elected. He has written:
As an appointed Chamber it simply does not carry the credibility to perform the role in this day and age.
If an elected Senate would be, as some people fear, an example of the cure being worse than the disease because it contradicts the principle of Cabinet Government, then we must attempt another kind of reform, namely, one that will spell out clearly and definitively that the Senate's role is not to hold a veto over this House but to assist it precisely by refining its legislation and making major studies of current problems. If that is what history has shown the legitimate role of the Senate as an appointed body should be, then let the Constitution say so. Let us make a reform that spells out in words and legislation the way history has evolved.
I plead that Hon. Members of the House see that reform of the Senate should not stop there. The Senate can never have credibility with the nation, with the House of Commons or perhaps even with itself as long as it is, as so many members of the public have thought it to be, a happy hunting ground for hacks, a plantation for patronage plums, a Shangri-La for sinecure seekers. If an elected Senate is not acceptable, then let us use the opportunity of having a new Government and a new Parliament to give Canada a new method for appointing Senators, one that will give them the same public respect
March 8, 1985

enjoyed by Justices of the Supreme Court who are appointed without reference to partisan criteria.
To quote the Hon. Robert Stanfield on the Senate:
We should do whatever is in our power to increase its credibility and that has to come basically through reform of the appointment process.
I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that the time has come for this House to endorse a resolution calling upon the Government to initiate a process that will lead to legislation reforming the Senate and making it a more viable, credible, effective and acceptable institution in our parliamentary system.
I must conclude by saying that if such reforms are not possible, then I as one Member of Parliament would have to believe that abolition is the only reasonable alternative. An unelected legislature exercising powers to make and unmake laws has no place in a democracy. As the Leader of the Opposition in this House has written, "... the argument for its abolition is difficult to resist". Only legitimate and adequate reform can resist it.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate this afternoon on a motion to reform the Senate. One cannot help but wonder if this is not indeed a motion rather to abolish the Senate, a move which seems to be a late bluff of some of the Conservative Members of this House.
When the Senate is accused of not doing its job, we say it needs reform. When it is accused of doing its job, we say it needs to be abolished. It is that kind of schizophrenic behaviour on the part of some Conservative Members of the House that makes me wonder if we know what we are speaking about.
1 do not purport to be an expert on constitutional matters in this country, but it seems to me that throughout the years, the Senate of the country, nothwithstanding the fact that it does require reform, has indeed performed a very unique and useful role. Let us look at some of the history of that institution.
When the Provinces of Canada East and Canada West joined together along with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, there was fear in Canada East, which prior to that was called Lower Canada, that through representation by population, the parliamentary structures would create a circumstance under which the Francophone group of Lower Canada may eventually lose its reprensentation through sheer numbers. Therefore, the people of Canada East wanted to have a structure by which there would be a guaranteed representation, and that structure of course was the Senate. It is also interesting to note that in the Province of Quebec, unlike any other province, the Senate has electoral districts or Senate ridings, if we can call them that.
Again, looking at this matter historically, we also note that the maritime provinces wanted to have some guarantees that they would not be part of the conflict that was raging at that time between Canada East and Canada West. There were linguistic conflicts and a constant deadlock after the Act of Union of 1840, and there seemed to be a new Government
The Senate
about once a year. The maritime provinces felt that difficulties could arise from the union because they felt they had more stable parliamentary institutions at that time. Again, they wanted a structure which would guarantee some uniformity, consistency and regional representation. That structure, of course, was the Senate.
We are discussing here today whether or not the Senate accomplished any useful role in providing regional balance to this country.
If I remember correctly, Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker said that he thought the Senate had not fulfilled its mandate to represent the regions of this country. I would like to remind my Conservative colleagues how, after the 1979 election when the Clark Government had only one Member from Quebec, a Francophone, who could be appointed to Cabinet, how the then Prime Minister decided to have a Francophone presence from Quebec in Cabinet. Mr. Speaker, I would remind the House that Messrs. Asselin, Flynn and de Cotret were appointed to the Senate to guarantee the Province of Quebec representation in Cabinet, because there was no other way to do so at the time.
Perhaps the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse), who spoke earlier, feels that those Senators did not do a good job in Cabinet. That may be his opinion, but I think that although the Government of that day was shortlived, it was essential that Quebec be adequately represented in Cabinet, and that is the mechanism that was used at the time.

We are told that as an institution of sober second thought the Senate has not been useful. In the opinion of the Hon. Member who has just spoken, it was the fault of the Senate that the War Measures Act was invoked. I would like to remind the Hon. Member that his Party voted for the War Measures Act as well as did the Government of the time.
They did not stop it.

Well, I have not taken the time today to verify how Conservative Senators voted on that Bill, but I know that the Conservative Members of the House-who, the Member claims, were pure and holier than thou-voted for that Bill. In hindsight we might say that the measure was unnecessary, but we are not debating that today. We are debating the fact that the Conservative Members of the House of Commons also voted for that Bill, and now the Conservative Party is accusing Liberal Senators because they voted for it.
I think I have just described what is wrong with the Government. It is trying to find scapegoats for its incompetence. Conservative Members have indicated that the War Measures Act was the fault of Liberal Senators, even though Conservative Members of the House voted for that measure. Today,

March 8, 1985
The Senate
because of the Government's inability to run the country, to keep interest rates down, and to find employment, it is creating a new debate-the debate of the Senate.
The Senate does need to be reformed. We have probably looked at Senate reform in Canada since 1868-just after the institution was established. There have been Liberal and Conservative Governments since that time. There is no reason for the Member who has just spoken to stand and say that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) should act on it now. Since when is it the initiative of the Leader of the Opposition to initiate government legislation? Introducing government legislation, in my short experience in the House, was, I thought, the responsibility of the Government. That is why it is called government legislation. Perhaps the Hon. Member should become familiar with that fact. What we have today is nothing but a red herring. Conservative Members of the House are attacking another institution because of their own inability to govern.
The Government House Leader (Mr. Hnatyshyn) was quoted in The Globe and Mail of today as having said:
You can't abolish the Senate without unanimity, the reason being that it affects the amending formula under the Constitution.
He also said that it would require the consent of all ten provinces, as well as the consent of the House. But the Member opposite just told us that it required the initiative of the Leader of the Opposition. Need I remind that Hon. Member of the feelings of the ultra-conservative Premier of British Columbia? How does the Premier of B.C. feel about abolishing the Senate? How do the other Premiers in Canada feel about abolishing the Senate? They do not feel that it needs to be done away with-
How does your Leader feel about it?

I am glad the Hon. Member asked how I felt about the Senate. I feel that our parliamentary institutions need to be enhanced, protected and, first and foremost, they need to be respected by each and every one of us.

And that, Mr. Speaker, is where the Members of this House have been extremely remiss. We must remember that senators are Members of Parliament as we are. We are Members of Parliament as Members of the House of Commons, and Senators are Members of the Parliament of Canada by the very fact they have been appointed to the Senate.
That is not true!

One of the Members opposite says that a Senator is not a Member of Parliament. He is entitled to his opinion, but I would strongly advise him to read the Constitution of our country and to become a bit better acquainted with our parliamentary procedure. If he has ever presented a petition in this House or in the past read up on the history and traditions of the Parliament of this country, Mr.Speaker-The Parliament of Canada is not the House of Commons, it is the
Governor General representing the Queen, the Senate and the House of Commons in assembly. I want to mention and emphasize that for the information of the Hon. Member opposite who has just stated that a senator is not a member of Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, some claim that the Senate has not played an important role, especially over the past few years, and that it has not carried out its duties in the best interests of the Canadian people. I could mention a number of achievements and reports . . . For instance, "Soil At Risk" is an excellent report which has been prepared by the Senate and which several Hon. Members of the House have publicly described as being a well-documented paper of major significance. There have been in the past many such documents. The Senate of our country has done quite a lot of work in many areas.

The Senate has acted as a Chamber of sober second thought.
Prove it.

There are some New Democratic Members who say that it is not useful and that it is unnecessary. Perhaps they should review some of the Bills which have been passed by the Senate to see what they missed when the Bills were in the House. Then they will know that their shortcomings are sometimes corrected by the expertise which exists in the upper Chamber of our Parliament.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I will say that I feel it is somewhat ironic that we are debating this motion today. We have today, very appropriately, discussed women's issues in this House. I live in the same village as the first woman Senator of this country, Senator Cairine Wilson, who was appointed to the Senate in 1930 and whose statue is right here in this building. I just thought that on this particular day it was appropriate to pay a special tribute to the first woman ever to have sat in that illustrious Chamber, namely, the Hon. Senator, Cairine Wilson.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind my Progressive Conservative colleagues that the steps taken by the Senate in recent weeks were aimed at delaying an unreasonable initiative on the part of the Government. Unreasonable indeed, for the Government came before this House to ask the Canadian Parliament to approve expenditures for a fiscal year yet to begin, a fiscal year for which the estimates had not even been tabled. Mr. Speaker, we have seen today why we do need the Senate, if only to remind the House and, particularly, the Progressive Conservative Party that Canada is not under a dictatorship and that respect must be shown for our parliamentary institutions. So it was the Senate which reminded the Progressive Conservative Government about the respect which our parliamentary institutions command.
March 8, 1985

Mr. Speaker, one of the NDP Members was wondering why the Bill left this Elouse in the first place. I thought that any NDP Member would know and recall that, on December 21, when the Bills came up for debate in the House on the last sitting day, we reached a compromise and agreed to hold a debate on universality and another one on a Conservative Measure which threatened a tradition and something important to this country. On that day, the House had to debate that measure and, once this was done, the Bill was read the third time and sent to the Senate.
I would remind my NDP colleague that Liberal Members rose to speak in the House on many occasions, and I challenge him to check that in Hansard. He will find out that it was not only in the Senate that Liberal Members or rather members of the Liberal Party stressed the importance of seeing the Government's estimates before passing the Bill, for I said so myself in my speech when the Bill was under consideration.
As usual, we see that the preconceived ideas of the New Democratic Party and of the Progressive Conservative Party, which of late seem to have been drawing closer than before-

We are seeing, Mr. Speaker, more and more members of the Conservative and New Democratic Parties sleeping in the same bed. On this particular issue it is quite obvious again. We are seeing this incestuous relationship, and let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that it is becoming obvious that the two Parties are playing the same game in this House.
The New Democratic Party does not want a Senate. Perhaps it does not feel that the regional interests of this country are important. I accept that as the policy of those Hon. Members, if that is the policy they wish to have. But I don't like it and I feel that that is why that Party will never get anywhere. But Hon. Members of the Conservative Party should know better. They are in government. They should have more respect for our parliamentary institution. If they do not realize the value of our institutions, Mr. Speaker, then let them consult with the provincial Premiers across the country. Let them ask what those Premiers think of this initiative, and we will see that that idea will be soundly defeated. Reform of the Senate, Mr. Speaker, yes; abolition of the Senate, definitely not.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on the motion of the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse). It is a possible sign that there might be some action at last on this subject, which everyone says has been talked about for the whole history of the entity known as Canada, then a semi-independent country and now a "maybe" independent country. It depends on whether we can run our own affairs without interference from across the border.
This motion only calls for reform of the Senate, but I would like to support it in the hope that an exploration of reform might lead sooner or later-I hope sooner-to the discovery that reform is neither possible nor really useful and that the only real alternative is abolition.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Of course, that has always been the policy of the Party I represent, including its predecessor since 1933. The Hon. Member opposite who said, "Hear, hear!" reminded me previously of his history in that connection.
He must be a red Tory.

The CCF adopted this policy in 1933. I was not at that convention. I was a little too young, but I will admit that that was one of the many attractive features of the CCF when I joined it in 1957. Since then I have never had any occasion to reconsider or have second thoughts about the proposal to abolish the Senate, to reform it right out of existence.
The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), said that the Senate has done many good jobs on legislation, but he did not say what jobs. I am not aware of any Bill which came out of the Senate any better than it went in. There have been some Bills, such as Bills concerned with regulation of the banks, which came out from the Senate worse than when they went in. That is not surprising considering the ties and directorships which many members of the Senate have.
There was a Bill put forward by the Liberal Government last year to impose the secret service on us, the CSIS, which did go to the Senate and did get a superficial proposal for reform. However, it was clear by the actions of the Liberal Government that it was not interested in having that Bill improved. It was only interested in playing for time. It only used the Senate as a smoke-screen in order that it could ram the Bill through the following year with only superficial and cosmetic changes. Some of the changes which in fact the Senate committee suggested were ignored by the Government. It was clear, therefore, that the Government of the day did not intend that the Senate should actually improve the Bill. It only intended that the Senate be part of a charade in the pretense of the Government that it was consulting the public on a Bill to impose a secret police on us that was utterly irresponsible, that is to say, it has absolutely no obligation to report what it is doing to any elected representative of Canada.
The Senate made no change in that essential irresponsibility of the Bill in its proposals, so the whole charade of putting it to a Senate Committee was, as I say, only a way of keeping it out of public view for some months, then bringing it back with deceptive changes made. They changed nothing fundamentally. So I am very pleased that there are no New Democrats in the Senate. There are certainly New Democrats who have been respected enough by the Government of the day that they might have been appointed to the Senate, but if they were ever asked, they declined. There are now no New Democrats in the Senate, and therefore, as The Toronto Sun points out, we are in a very clear position in saying it should be abolished. I hope there never will be New Democrats in the Senate. There will

be New Democrats on the other side of the House in due course, but not in the Senate.
It is very interesting to note that The Toronto Sun is with us. It surprises Paul Godfrey, the Editor. It even surprises us a little bit, but not as much as it surprises him, because we believe that our position was sound and that some day even publications such as The Toronto Sun will recognize that. Evidently some Members across the way are beginning to recognize the soundness of our position. They were probably encouraged to do that by the extreme action in the opposite direction of the previous Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, in entrenching the Senate into the Constitution and then loading it down with his buddies just before he left and just after he left with the little deal he made with his successor. That certainly left a bad taste in the mouths of many Canadians. That, of course, is no reflection on the individual merits of the Members of the other place, but it is a reflection on the function that that body has served, intentionally or unintentionally.
I congratulate the Member for Scarborough West for having introduced this subject. I would be very interested to know whether he and his colleagues, who have votes in this place, are serious about what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) has trumpeted in the media in the last few weeks, what many of his colleagues on that side of the House have supported, and what the Hon. Member for Scarborough West advocates in his motion. Are they really going to try to make changes?
The Hon. Member for Scarborough West reminded us that a former Prime Minister, John Diefenbaker, said that everybody talks about Senate reform like the weather but nobody does anything about it. In that case, John Diefenbaker himself was one of the nobodies, that is to say, he did nothing about it. He had a term of office in which he could have addressed the matter, but apparently he did not choose to do so. Now the members of this Party are talking about the need to do something. The question is whether they are serious or whether this is just horseplay. I am sure the Hon. Member for Scarborough West is serious, but he is a back-bencher. He sits as close to the back-benches on his side as I do on my side. It is not clear whether those who sit on the front benches share his seriousness of purpose.
Is the Cabinet willing to proceed or is it just stalling? Is it going to put forward a definite, concrete proposal, or perhaps even a Bill as a beginning? If not a Bill, will it make a report to Parliament? Will it put a motion to the appropriate committee of Parliament to have this matter opened up? In the alternative, will it hide behind the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner)? Is it going to say that with 211 votes in the House it cannot do it because 40 people on the opposite side of the House in the Liberal caucus are not going to co-operate?
If the Prime Minister takes that stand seriously he will make himself the laughing-stock of the country. Everybody
can count. Everyone knows that if the Prime Minister wants to put that through the House of Commons, he can do it. There is a constitutional question which he might have thought of before he spoke, but perhaps, as is his custom, he is better at speaking than at thinking, and he does not always know which he should do first. The fact is that he said he was going to make changes, and then the next day he and his colleagues began to wonder whether it was possible to make the changes. The fact is that there are colleagues of his Party in most of the provincial Governments of Canada. If there is agreement within his Party, they can act.
I can assure him, on the basis of more than 50 years of consistent policy by the NDP and the CCF, that he will not find the Government of Manitoba difficult to work with on this point. I can assure him that he will have co-operation from the Premier of Manitoba. There is evidently the potential for near unanimity among the provincial Governments of the country. Changes in the Constitution have been accomplished before with even less unanimity than that.
The question raised by the motion of the Hon. Member for Scarborough West is whether this talk by the Prime Minister and others of his Party about reforming the Senate is merely a dodge to take the minds of the public off the fact that the Conservative Government is doing nothing about jobs and tax reform, or whether it is a serious concern that will be followed up in the next week or two by a substantial proposal from the Prime Minister or one of his colleagues in the Cabinet for actual reform of the Senate. We will soon know whether the Conservatives are serious about it or are just leaving a backbencher out to dry.

Mr. Speaker, it is a real pleasure for me to have the opportunity this afternoon to speak in support of this motion on Senate reform which was put forward by my colleague and roommate, the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse). This is a subject on which I personally have felt very strongly for a long time. In my very first year of university, I took a Canadian political science course. After having taken that course, I was convinced that we needed some very drastic changes in the Canadian Senate. Therefore, I am delighted to have this opportunity to speak today on that very subject, which takes me back a few years.
The subject of Senate reform has been discussed very broadly and in a great deal of detail over a number of years. The pace of that debate has been speeding up, particularly in the years leading up to our new Constitution, our new amending formula, and our new Charter of Rights. Since that time, there has been a great deal of debate on what we should do about the Canadian Senate.
There are a variety of thoughts which I believe break down into four main choices. The first choice is that of making some modifications in the power of the Senate. The second choice is that of changing the method of selection of appointees to the Senate, or changing the method of appointment. The third choice is the possibility of actually having an elected Senate, as my friend the Hon. Member for Scarborough West suggested.
March 8, 1985

The fourth choice is, as both the Hon. Member for Scarborough West and the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) indicated, that of abolishing the Senate altogether.
With regard to modification of the Senate, or any of these choices, the key to the issue is accountability, that is, whether the Senate is an accountable body now or whether it can be made an accountable body and whether, in a democracy, we can have a body which is not accountable to the people of the country.
With regard to the first option of modifying the powers of the Senate, there is no question in my mind that no matter what is done with the Senate, whether its power to block legislation is limited or whether a time limit is imposed on its debate, it still cannot be made accountable to the people of the country. Therefore, I personally reject the idea of tampering with the powers of the Senate.
The second possibility is to have another method for Senate appointments, that is, based on propositions put forward by provincial Premiers that the provinces be allowed to appoint people to the Senate. Once again, this raises a very basic and fundamental issue about the accountability of the Senate to the people of the country. Tampering with the powers of the Senate or finding another method to appoint Senators, be it by the provinces or anyone else, does not deal with their accountability and responsibility to the people of Canada.
The third choice that is possible, which has been suggested today, is that of electing the Senate. I reject that proposal because it would bring about a very fundamental change in the concept of our democratic government and Canadian parliamentary system. As the Hon. Member for Scarborough West has pointed out, our system is a Cabinet system in which the Cabinet is responsible to the House. If there is more than one elected body, there will be two bodies claiming to have equal accountability and responsibility to the people of this country. They will be vying to represent the authority of those points of view as far as Canadians are concerned. I do not believe that will work and I think it would simply create a stalemate. It could very well happen that an elected body in this House and in the other House could have differing views on how the country should be run, and if so, both these elected bodies could claim to have the right to follow their respective course, based on the mandate they received from Canadians. I suggest that we do not want that.
What we have had in the past in this country is strong government. When the Government must act, it has had the ability to act because of the Cabinet and the parliamentary system. That is not the case in every democracy. France went through many republics before de Gaulle became President. The main reason that France could not come to grips with its problems was the instability of the constitutional system under which it was operating. We would not want to move from a system with one unelected, unrepresentative House, to a system with two, which would create a completely unstable
The Senate
government in this country. Personally, I believe we would be extremely foolish to adopt such a system.
It has been suggested that perhaps we could modify the powers of the Senate in relation to having an elected body there. At the same time, Senator Pitfield, whom my hon. friend quoted, also said that it would not be possible to limit the powers of another responsible and elected body for long because it would also have a mandate from the people.
The fourth choice, which I believe is the only choice, is that the Senate must in fact be abolished. It seems to me that when we look at the history of Canadian parliamentary democracy and try to find the isolated events when the Senate played a role of which we can be proud, the only one I can think of is the James Coyne affair. He is the former President of the Bank of Canada who came into conflict with the Government of the day. The Senate took his side in that argument and there was a great controversy in the country about whether or not the Government had the right to tell the Governor of the Bank of Canada how to run the monetary policy of the country. As a result of that Coyne affair, the Governor of the Bank resigned from his position. The question of whether the Government had the power to direct monetary policy was left in Limbo temporarily. Subsequently, a new Government with a majority in the Senate decided that the Government should have that power, and it changed the Bank of Canada Act so that it is now clear that Mr. Coyne's position was not the one we wanted in the country and that the Government of Canada should have that power.
Many people in various provinces have said in recent days that it would be foolish to abolish the Senate. There was a day when many provinces of this country had a second House of Legislature. Today, there is not one. In fact, the provinces abolished all of their legislative second Houses, and if they believed that the second legislative body was so essential to their proceedings it is almost inconceivable that they would believe we should not abolish the Senate of Canada.
Therefore, I am led inevitably to the conclusion that our Senate should be abolished and that this motion should be passed to call upon the Government to take some action in this manner.
What action can the Government take once the motion is passed? The Constitution Act sets out provisions for amending the Constitution of the country and the method for dealing with the Senate and any motion to abolish, or otherwise reform, the Senate. Those provisions are set out in Section 38(1) of the Act, as well as in Section 41 and Section 42.
Section 38(1) provides the power to pass a motion of the House of Commons. The remaining procedure is outlined, but my time is drawing to an end. I want to ensure that this motion comes to a vote this afternoon, and with that in mind, I urge you, Mr. Speaker, to put the motion to a vote right now.

HOUSE OF COMMONS CHAMBER, OTTAWA on Thursday, March 7, 1985
